[Main Text]
It is said that when a person has a pterygium (ẓafara) in their eye, they should look toward the South Pole and toward Canopus (Suhayl). If it begins during the month of Virgo (Sunbula), it will be completely gone within forty-nine nights.

Altogether, there are twenty-eight lunar mansions in detail. Let me explain so that the principle becomes known, and here is the detail of that principle:

The Arabs and desert dwellers, since ancient times, reckoned their calendar by the appearance of the crescent moon. But this system proved inconsistent — sometimes falling in summer, sometimes in winter. In order to properly regulate the solar year, they adopted solar reckoning so they could know the seasons of the year. In relation to these seasons, they needed to attend to pasturelands and wintering grounds, staying in their lowland pastures when appropriate. They needed to observe the conditions overhead, and they found that the celestial sphere passes over a fixed number of days and nights per segment. They saw that in two nights at the end of a month the moon becomes invisible; accordingly they dropped those nights from the count and divided the visible circuit of the celestial sphere into twenty-eight parts. Each part they called a mansion (manzil), and they said the moon occupies one of these mansions each night. They assigned a marker to each mansion so that one could be distinguished from another, and the scholars of the stars called this the "path of Qarah-Qar" [i.e., the method of Karokar/the zodiacal belt]. Of these twenty-eight mansions, fourteen rise in the east and set: sometimes they rise in the east and set in the west, some rising while others set, and fourteen are grouped as the "harmful" ones (manāzil al-ḍarr). Those that rise in the dawn and set in the evening set in the west while the opposite ones rise in the east. It ends with [the mansions of] al-Safar, al-Fargh, al-Qanb, al-Mughrib, al-Sāwila, and al-Bald.

...and from cold and frost. And when the lunar mansion is complete, it appears just as its equal and counterpart, and they are called the mansions of al-Sharatain. The last of them is al-Ghafr, and the first mansion is Nath, and when these mansions rise in the east and set in the west, this is a matter that cannot be fully understood in one year. Rather, know that the celestial sphere is divided into twelve parts, and the division of the zodiacal belt is into houses, and the division of its middle circle is into twenty-eight lunar mansions, and they are called the mansions of the stars. The difference between them is that the zodiacal houses are determined by the passage of the sun — as it were, the stars of the fixed mansions are arranged in order — and those are: "That is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing" [Quran 36:38]. Thus the Almighty God, exalted and glorified, created these things, and so the point of the equinox moves through each of the zodiac signs, and the lunar mansions of al-Sharatain occur, and they are close to the ecliptic, and they are called the first mansion — "Shadalankaro" and the mansions of Kasil — with their aspects and some of their states and some of their forms and some of their conditions, as is well-known among them: al-Sharatain. This station is sometimes called elevated and sometimes base, and it is called "Sharatan" in the sense of a sign or mark, meaning a sign for conditions and indications of states. Its two stars are located near the Pleiades, and they are faint and close together, spanning about one thousand units in measure. Their shadows fall to the north in the southern direction, and when the sun is among them at the two equinox seasons, they become equal. And when al-Sharatain rises, the parts of time become equal. Their counterpart star is light and swift in motion. These are to be considered as reference points for al-Sirat, and their form is thus: ••••• And the rising of this mansion...

When the color of the human being is at this point, it falls; when the Pleiades (Nathrah) rise in the eighth [station], it produces a kind of wonder. It disappears in time and its waters rise, and images increase, and it produces various types of bounty. The smallest of its forms settles in the belly, as is described: it is reckoned below the belly in proportion to the smallest. The hidden stars at that point, three of them appearing like stones — their foot-shape becomes apparent. When one night before Libra (Qalinji) rises, and one night before the beginning of Tishrin (October) has passed, one night of Libra's season — if the falling [of rain] does not occur, the descendants will be in distress, and kites and buzzards will come to the coasts, and ants will emerge from under stones. A kind of wonder is noted: when it is as if the sands are washed and the redness goes and the Arabs call these phenomena 'al-Anwa' (the star-rains). At its time, the winds blow and the streams run, and its setting and rising are well known. At that point, al-Hamal (Aries) ascends, and it is known that when it is in the middle, small grains scatter, and the observers say it is beyond telling. When many stars appear, or when rain falls at that time, abundance comes, meaning prosperity increases — this is according to the smallest of the Pleiades (Thurayya al-Sughra). The other form of it is that when it is plentiful, it means much wealth — that is its other form. So when it rises in the third part of Tishrin al-Akhir (late October) and falls, and when it rises in the east from Misr (Egypt), winter becomes apparent. And one night, the cold of mid-autumn comes, and winter remains and the rains come. Its rising is blessed, as the Prophet of God — peace be upon him — said: 'When the Pleiades rise, harm departs from every people.' That is, when the Pleiades (Thurayya) rise, calamity departs and the Arabs say this kind of wonder — rain after its rising is very beneficial, because the earth absorbs it and stores moisture within it, and what comes after the rising of the Pleiades: winter becomes apparent among the Arabs, as it is said: 'When the Pleiades rise, the seas surge and the winds clash and the sultan [of storms rules].'

The jinn dwell upon the waters. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: 'Whoever sails the sea after the rising of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) is absolved of responsibility' — meaning, whoever boards a ship after the rising of the Pleiades, God Almighty's protection withdraws from him [i.e., it is at one's own risk]. During the season of the Pleiades, the air becomes pleasant, the terrain becomes traversable, and horses thrive; toward its end, the Nile rises and sailors' livelihoods improve. Some say it is derived from the Arabic root meaning 'to scatter abundantly,' thus it was named accordingly. Others, reading it with a fatha, interpret it to mean 'the spreading of light,' saying it resembles the spreading of luminescence. After the Pleiades, the star Atū rises — it is considered a follower of the Pleiades — and with it are hidden stars. Their hidden configuration is as described in the diagram: ••••• The varieties of this lunar mansion are not limited; generally with its moisture come abundant rains, and in the first year the pastures dry up and the grasses wither, and its influence upon our region is great. The Arabs say: 'When al-Dabarān rises, the maidens are hindered' — meaning when the horn of al-Dabarān rises, the pastures wither, the eastern and simoom winds appear, grapes do not ripen. The rising of al-Dabarān is on the sixteenth of Aries, and its setting is on the sixth of the first Nisan [April]. The stars of al-Dabarān's group are called the Hyades; some call the reddish star among them 'Fal.' The seventeen stars around it are called al-Qalasr, and the heart of al-Dabarān is its apex. It is called 'the circle of the horse's back.' Al-Jawzāʾ consists of three stars, some close together in the shape of al-Baltān. It is named by the method of al-Tanbiha: its rising is on the ninth of Capricorn and its setting is on the twenty-ninth of that same sign. Its variety is noble — they say: 'When it rises over us, we cannot remain seated,' [such is its power].

And in the constellation [under discussion], according to the tradition, the rule and other authorities agree that when the poisonous wind (samum) blows, it is as though a dome of flame erupts. Its benefit [منفعه] is that the armies encamped beneath it will be [properly] guided in their movements, and whoever learns its principles will see and perceive [things]. The middle [pair] of its two stars is established and continues, one upon another, reaching beyond and descending. These stars surrounding it are like fifteen stars in it, arranged in the shape of the letters alif and ayn. Its rising [heliacal] is in the second [decade] of the heat of Haziran [June], and within it, at its highest peak, are clouds, vapors, winds of rain, and beneficial [influences]. And the fifth [mansion]: the Forearm (al-Dhira'), which is the Forearm of the Lion — its two stars, one grasped and one extended, [lie] on the Syria side and on the extended side: the mansion is the Grasped Forearm, and whoever sees it sees a shape like a bag, whose size [spans] as much as a measuring rod's length across. Its heliacal rising is on the fourth day of Tuz [a month name] and its setting is on the fourth day of Kanun al-thani [January]. In Turkish it is called [lü-köy köngülünde ndibeh]. The Arabs say: 'The Forearm has risen, the Dhira'[constellation] is brilliant.' And it resides in such-and-such a town, being the ninth [station]. Its essence: two winds come and blow from the north, bearing those who dwell beneath it, one after another by a span's distance, seeing [stars] and also seeing auspicious [things] at their midpoint. Its form is thus. Its heliacal rising is in [the month] when it appears at Badlis, and its setting is at the end of [the month] of Kanun [December]. [The constellation] is of the nature of Sa'd al-Dhabih [the Lucky Star of the Slaughterer], being the 109th [in order]. Look to it: it means two stars like the Furqan [a pair], one measure apart — if you look carefully, you will find it — the eye of Leo passes through it. Its rising is in the month of Aba [Av/August] and its setting is in the month of Kanun al-thani [January]. Its form is thus.

When Mahmud appears in Cancer, it benefits greatly; poisons are neutralized, horses grow lean, and they increase by night and day. The nights lengthen, and in the autumn season the companion star rises in its second degree, which is beneficial. When the star of Burj al-Zaldar (the Lesser) is present in the center position, it shows moderate characteristics according to its form. 

The rising occurs on the fourth day and the setting of Shabakl occurs on the fourth day; of this, the chief Mahmud in Cancer, when present, indicates abundant vegetation and trees inclining toward the northwest, and the companion is Sa'd al-Su'ud, and its branch follows. In wounds from iron blows, when they pass through, those in the lesser position proceed until healed. 

Between them the rulings and stable observations are to be noted, and they are matched in their phase. The Lesser Bear rises in one position and sets in Adhar in another position. The chief Mahmud brings much rain; orchards become cool, moisture increases, and its companion is in the Hadi position, and its second letter follows. This appears in the Lesser Burj when it reaches Zuhra; its form appears. This Moon is in the opposition of Zuhra; the heart of Leo disperses coldness and its setting disperses heat toward Leo. 

The rising is in the month of Elul, on the third day, and the setting is in the month of Adhar in the first days, and its days grow cold as Naylaart returns, and the companion is Fara' Muqaddam, and its pair is 'Awa — in exchange and proportion. Its meaning relates to the positions of the stars; the word 'Lam' means that no one among Naʿm and Bala in its direction... They settled in Kalbalde, sent toward Arslan, gathered against them, and it is called so. The rising is on the twenty-eighth of Elul and the setting is on the twenty-eighth of Adhar, and the chief Mahmud — its companion is Fara' Mu'akhkhar and its fourth is Sak, and this is Sak, the single 'Azl.

Without its counterpart [i.e., Unoccupied / solo], near Tawnak, there is no smoky star; however, near the Spear-bearer Simak (Arcturus), there is a smoky star. That smoky star is between the two, between the Unarmed Simak and the Spear-bearing Simak, standing roughly equidistant. Its form is that of a figure. • The rising of Tawnak is at the end of the first decade of Tishrin (October), and its setting is on the fourth of Nisan (April). Its nature is powerful; it rarely occurs with pestilence or harm. And the twenty-seventh [mansion] is al-Ghafr — with a fatḥa on the ghayn and sukūn on the fāʾ — meaning its opposite; it consists of three dim stars in the constellation Virgo. •• They call it al-Ghafr (the cover/concealment) because its rising coincides with the great star Mizar becoming hidden from sight, growing distant, and the Ghafr stars themselves are dim stars hidden from observation, growing distant. Its rising is on the twenty-eighth of Tishrin (October) and its setting is on the sixteenth of Nisan (April). Its nature is that of Sharṭā. The twenty-eighth mansion is al-Zubānā — with a fatḥa on the zāʾ, meaning 'the claws' — and the two stars of it are like Tir (Mercury); they are called the horns of Scorpio. Their number in Karshakar's reckoning is [given]. • Its rising is at the end of Tishrin (October) and its setting is at the end of Nisan (April). Under its nature, the people of the settled lands and the surrounding regions enter into difficulties and hardship. The twenty-ninth mansion is al-Iklīl (the Crown), meaning its opposite; it consists of four stars forming the head of Scorpio, and it is also called the other Karshakar. • Its rising falls in the eighth of Tishrin (October) and its setting is on the tenth of Bārkil (November); under its nature, horses wander until the belly of Ḥūt (Pisces) rises, and horses are not found. The twenty-eighth [star] is Qalb [al-Aqrab] (Heart of the Scorpion): a single bright star, and near it are two other stars also called Ṣanw, one of which is somewhat above and the other somewhat below.

Its shape is thus: It is called Qalb al-Aqrab [Heart of the Scorpion]. Its heliacal rising occurs on the sixth day of the last Tishrin [November], and its setting is on the sixth day of Iyar [May]. Its benefit is well-known: if one reaches that water it dries up. Its opposing star is in Diran, the twenty-ninth [star], which is called Shawl, in Fitshan, and it runs along.

The meaning of 'Scorpio's depth': In it there are stars close together, resembling one another — for this reason it is called 'the strength of Scorpio.' Therefore it appears elevated in the north, below Thawr [Taurus], and its shape is thus. Its rising is on the twenty-second of Kanun al-Awwal [December], and its setting occurs on the first days of the entering of Iyar [May]. Its benefit for that vicinity is that trees produce fruit, pastures grow, and orchards bear. Its opposing star is of great benefit, the second [in rank]. It is called the name for a camel's growl. And the ninth of the sheep's orbit is called thus, and these seven stars are exactly opposite the Milky Way. In it the melodies that arrive are said to be from the Milky Way; the melodies that issue out are said to come from what exits the Milky Way. The melodies proceeding are said to be below [the track of] the Milky Way, having emerged from beneath it, just as the outer [stars] resemble the shape of a bowl.

Its shape is thus: ... Its rising is on the twenty-fifth of Kanun al-Awwal [December], and its setting is on the twenty-fifth of entering Iyar [May]. Its benefit in that period: days and nights become equal, and its opposing star is of benefit, the twentieth [in rank], a gift. Hope arises and the melodies dissipate and are lost. There is no star in the Milky Way [at this point]; a faint star appears there. It goes with Kawch [?] in Libra and some stars are in Qaws [Sagittarius] in that manner, and its shape appears thus.

.... Its rising is at the end of Kanun al-Akhir [late January], and its setting is at the end of Tawz [Tammuz/July]. In its period of benefit, the twenty-sixth [star] is Sa'd Dhabih [the Lucky Stars of the Slaughterer]. In it small stars appear at its setting. From it, toward the north by about one cubit, no star appears along the Milky Way, but to the south there are rays in the direction of the south.

And among the small stars that appear in Arabia, there are sheep — that is what they call this asterism. Its form resembles that. Its heliacal rising is on the seventeenth of the last month of winter (Kanun al-Akhir), and its setting is on the seventeenth of Tammuz. In its season the trees draw up water, Adam-trees and Zughaj-trees begin to move, and its mansion is Nathrah.

The second and third [star] is Sa'd al-Dhabi': it moves through the sky equal to the greater [star] and surpasses it. Its form is like the greater Suhail of the south, and one may call it the eraser. Its form is thus. From this point it is named Nizam. When it rises in the middle of the last Kanun, on the twenty-ninth day of that month it sets; and when it sets, in the month of Ab on its twenty-ninth. In its season onions, garlic, and meats grow strong, and salt, good things, and wind come from the south; its mansion faces Tarfah, and the second and third is Sa'd al-Su'ud. The sum of its stars: the seven of the Crown — such is its form. The source of its provision is Nizam, the source of its people and their livelihood, and the Arabs call this auspicious, giving food for its sake, therefore it is named. Its rising is on the twenty-second of Shubat and its setting on the fourteenth of Ab. The stars are gathered, and all the trees shed their leaves; starlings come, storks return from Rum, monks withdraw, and the days shorten.

The fifth [asterism] is Sa'd al-Akhbiyah: it lies in all directions, four stars like a hunter's form — thus. Its naming is Nizam.

When the red [stars] move in the land of desolation, for that reason it is named, therefore. Its rising is on the twenty-fifth of Shubat and its setting on the fourth of Ab. Its season is gathered thus: buffaloes drink water, chains are cut, its mansion is Zubarah, and the second is al-Tabani. Here, read and ponder — here, ponder the introduction of Fargh.

And another [star group] called Farghana: it is said to be among the mansions of the lunar stations, and its stars are each about five cubits apart in appearance, resembling a form without clear shape.
They are used as a guide for travelers, for when they rise and set they indicate [the seasons]. Their rising is in the sign of Aries [Hamal], and their number is nine and twenty [29], and their setting occurs on the twenty-ninth [day], and within it are certain winds and vapors.
And its dome [culmination] is in the direction of Qara, and when Aries rises in the season called Akis [harvest time], and sets in Akis [the same], its culmination occurs in that period, and in it are hot winds called Shadar and Fughaa and Ragham.
This [mansion] is close to the Fish [Pisces], and when the constellation of the Fish [Hut] reaches its belly, it indicates that from the direction of the south, the star Shatir rises with it, and this signifies the occurrence of cold and the approach of winter.
As for its rising, it is on the fourth of Nisan [April], and its setting is on the fifth of Tishrin [October], and thereafter the nights grow longer and the days begin to shorten, and the stars called Balkak appear.
Abu Ishaq [the astronomer] says: its journey through the signs is seven [degrees] per mansion, and each mansion has ten stars [kawkab], and one of them, namely Jabba, exceeds [this]. It completes [its course] in sixty-five days, and the sun traverses the Greek [Roman] celestial sphere in that time. The Balkak [Pleiades] are well-known mansions, more recognized and familiar than [other] mansions among travelers.
Know that the first of the Niza [lunar mansion markers] is a road leading to the treasury [Khazina], and from there seek [the next]. In that celestial sphere, on the northern side, go one day's measure and then seek the Two Conditions [Shartayn]. Then from that celestial sphere go westward one day's measure and from there seek Butayn. Then [go] toward the mansion Niza, and the Two Conditions, note well.

After the rank of these mansions has been established, one becomes able to understand the remaining mansions — indeed, like the path of the moon. Regarding the eastern and western regions, it is not a simplification to say that the mansions pass through each zodiac sign in a certain number of nights. It was mentioned in Tawqaruda that sometimes it passes through the eight mansions quickly and sometimes slowly — sometimes completing half the day's distance in one mansion, sometimes reaching the third mansion by midday, sometimes completing a mansion in half a day, and sometimes at midday it falls short by a fraction. When the celestial sphere divides into twelve zodiac signs, or sometimes into twenty-eight mansions proportionally, each zodiac sign receives its share of the mentioned mansions — one mansion, or a third of a mansion, and so on. When the moon passes through the mentioned mansions, it is as Ibn Ali indicated, and Ibn Ali also explained this elsewhere. Since it is of general benefit and complete utility, we mention it line by line, for when the moon is in:

Sharatayn: Travel is indicated; small trade is good; riding and commerce are favored; buying and selling are discouraged.

Butayn: Travel, treatment, seeking closeness, affection, and visiting are indicated; buying, selling, marriage, and cultivation are discouraged.

Thurayyā: Trade, hunting, work, reconciliation, and companionship are indicated; cold is expected; buying, selling, and cultivation are discouraged.

Dabarān: Building, neighboring, ownership of property, and associating with rulers and notables is indicated; treatment, socializing, and travel are discouraged.

Haqʿa: Marriage, buying, selling, and hunting are indicated; treatment, eating, and cultivation are discouraged.

Hanʿa: Sea travel, engaging with rulers, and felling trees are indicated; building and dealing with treasuries and royal affairs are discouraged.

Qira' (the 1st lunar mansion): It is good for seducing two opponents, for trade, for maintaining the king's guards, for calling a physician, and for companionship.
Nathra (the 5th lunar mansion): It is good for treatment, for hardship, for travel, for eating and drinking, and it brings an enemy to submission, for marriage arrangements and for work/business.
Tarfa (the 6th lunar mansion): It is good for war at sea, for travel, for accumulating wealth, for trade, for completing transactions, for marriage, and for making acquaintances.
Jabha (the 10th lunar mansion): It is good for agriculture and gardening, for buying and selling, for bringing love, and for travel and trust.
Zubra (the 11th lunar mansion): It is good for bringing abundance, for buying and selling, for partnerships, for cupping/bloodletting, and for good companionship.
Sarfa (the 12th lunar mansion): It is good for construction, agriculture, weddings, adornment, and for bringing the king's neighbors; it is good for sea travel and for the king's slaves.
'Awwa (the 13th lunar mansion): It is good for construction, agriculture, building, and treatment; it brings sea voyages, trade, and the freeing of slaves.
Simak (the 14th lunar mansion): It is good for sea travel, for noble deeds, and for clever stratagems; it brings trade and the fulfillment of needs.
Ghafr (the 15th lunar mansion): It is good for the king's slaves and servants, for preparing drinks and syrups, for education; it brings marriage, travel, and partnerships.
Zabana (the 16th lunar mansion): It is good for clothing, for the king's subjects and grains; it brings travel, buying and selling, trade, and companionship.
Iklil (the 17th lunar mansion): It is good for the king's horses, for syrups, and for sea travel; it brings buying and selling, dispatching messengers, and conquering.
Qalb (the 18th lunar mansion): It is good for the king's advisors and for gardening; it brings fortification of kingdoms and setting things in motion.
Shawla (the 19th lunar mansion): It is good for bringing abundance, for preparing drinks and syrups, and for the king's neighbors; it brings good companionship, travel, and partnerships.
Ma'im (the 20th lunar mansion): It is good for buying and selling, for seclusion and companionship; it brings travel, partnership, and agreements.
Balda (the 21st lunar mansion): It is good for servants, horses, the king's companions, ministers, and commanders; it brings travel, trade of slaves, and special affairs.
Dhabih (the 22nd lunar mansion): It is good for treatment, trade, building, ministers, and the king's servants; it brings good companionship and marriage.
Sal' (the 23rd lunar mansion): It is good for travel, companionship, and intimacy; it brings the king's satisfaction, prosperity, trade, and special matters.

Sa'd (Fortunate Stars): These ten are good for treatment, celebration, building, and meeting people; travel and helping others is indicated.
Akhbiyah: These ten are good for treating eye ailments, dealing with great men, farming, and marriage; travel and neighboring are indicated.
Muqaddam: These ten are good for farming, marriage, celebration, and governance; travel, commerce, and settlement are indicated.
Mu'akhkhar: These ten are good for beginning treatment, undertaking works; travel with preparation and investigation is indicated.
Risha: These ten are good for unity, seeking requests and pleasures; enmity and obstacles are indicated.

The Tenth View: The Sphere of the Zodiac is in the form of the Sphere of the Signs, which is an independent sphere, unlike the other spheres. Rather, it has been mentioned that each star has its own dedicated sphere, and each sphere has two poles. Since each sphere revolves around its center, the first star revolves around the center of its sphere from which the result comes, and the star moves from east to west as the center moves — just as the sun's sphere revolves around its center.

Every star has two motions: one is its own (dhātī) motion, and one is the secondary (qasr) motion, each differing from the other. The natural motion completes itself in the night and the daytime, revolving around its two centers, attributed to the great spheres within which the secondary motion operates. Thus the sphere of the sun revolves around its center from west to east, coming to the great circle — and this is what they call the Ecliptic (Falak al-Burūj). After this, by hypothetical assumption, a great circle whose center is the center of the universe, and whose two poles are the north and south poles, is found — and that circle is called the Celestial Equator (Mu'addal al-Nahār).

When we assume that the circle of the Ecliptic intersects the Celestial Equator, it divides it into two halves at two opposite points: one point is called the Vernal Equinox (I'tidāl Rabī'ī) and the other the Autumnal Equinox (I'tidāl Kharīfī).

After that, consider also the point of the equator (equinox) and the point of the ecliptic (falak al-buruj). If you take the two opposite points of it, one to the north and one to the south — for example, the point of the summer solstice and, to the south, the point of the winter solstice — then these two circles of the ecliptic divide it into two equal halves. The first quarter is that which lies between the vernal equinox point and the summer solstice point; this is called the season of spring, for as long as the sun travels that arc it is spring. And the arc between the summer solstice point and the autumnal equinox point is called the season of summer, for as long as the sun traverses that arc it is summer. The third quarter, between the autumnal equinox point and the winter solstice point, is called the season of autumn, for as long as the sun is on that arc it is autumn. And the fourth arc, between the winter solstice point and the vernal equinox point, is called the season of winter, for as long as the sun is on that arc it is winter.

After that, if we assume two great circles passing through the poles of the ecliptic and through the spring point and its opposite, the summer point, they divide it into four equal parts, producing the cardinal divisions. And when we extend these to six circles, each of which cuts the world at two opposite points along the ecliptic, each division is called a zodiacal sign (burj). If we then subdivide each sign, each sign contains thirty degrees, and the total of the six great circles together amounts to sixty parts. Once this is established and understood — as has been noted — it is well known that the fixed-star sphere (falak al-thawābit) is considered in two divisions, and in each division there are stars of various shapes and forms as described by the sages. Each division has a figure (sūra) and a configuration by which it is distinguished, as has been laid out. The meaning of the expression 'such-and-such a star is in such-and-such a zodiacal sign' is that a great circle drawn through…

The straight line is assumed to pass through the center of the ecliptic, striking [a point], separating [it], and the sphere comes to meet it at the first intersection. Ptolemy stated that every circular motion revolves around [the axis], completing eighty-six thousand [units], and seven hundred per mile for each motion of the ecliptic. It encompasses nine thousand [units], passing through three hundred [divisions].

Eighty-eight thousand and three hundred and ten miles in latitude, and a sixth of a degree per mile in width, one thousand [units] passing through three hundred, one hundred [units], and forty-two and a third miles. This is the Eleventh Perspective, which is the sphere that the religious scholars call the Throne ('Arsh), and astronomers call it the Encompassing Sphere (al-Falak al-A'zam). It surrounds all other spheres, and the greatest sphere is below all the other spheres.

The Atlas sphere (Falak al-Atlas) is below it — within it is a star of such magnitude — and the spheres move from east to west, opposite to the other spheres. The Atlas sphere moves along two opposite points: one toward the south pole and one toward the north pole, completing one revolution in a set period of hours. Its motion carries all the spheres and the stars in their motion.

Some have said this is because the greatest sphere is the container whose motion produces the observed movement, like a vessel carrying what is within it. This is what they have said, and the correct understanding is that the elements and the earth are encompassed within it — this is the proper explanation. The motion belongs to the bodies, not to the Exalted God. The greatest sphere has been given a force by which it moves, and the spheres within it are capable of moving anywhere — reaching near and far — and the greatest sphere moves. This motion, as the geometers have observed, is like the motion of the sun. That is to say, it is [a distance of] eight hundred farsakhs, and this is a proof of the correctness of the meaning, as shall be demonstrated.

It is reported and has come down to us: One day the Prophet, peace be upon them both, asked Gabriel about the time of prayer. Gabriel said: 'Do you not know? Come, I will show you.' On that day the sun had already traveled a distance of five hundred farsakhs in its movement. Rather, the sun performs its essential motion (al-haraka al-dhātiyya) from west to east, completing one full revolution around the greatest sphere (al-falak al-a'ẓam) in twenty-four hours, moving in its compelled motion (al-haraka al-qahriyya) from east to west. It turns from right to left, little by little, so that from left to right it proceeds as if gently, continuously, without ceasing, in opposition — and it is thus established that day and night arise from the motion of the greatest sphere. When the sun rises, as this sphere revolves, that side of the earth facing it is illuminated and brightened, and the living creatures there are moved toward it, and seeds sprout and plants grow and birds sing. But on the side away from it, as this sphere turns, the earth is dark and its air gloomy, and animals are still and plants dormant — until the sphere again moves and brings life back. The world continues in this orderly state of affairs. As the Almighty God, exalted and glorified, has said: 'And We have made the night a garment and the day for livelihood' (Qur'an 78:10-11). And in another place He says: 'And of His mercy He has made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein, and that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may give thanks' (Qur'an 28:73). Most astronomers hold that beyond the greatest sphere there is nothing further — and this is a corrupt belief, for beyond it, they say, there is neither void nor plenum. As for the most eminent of the later scholars, Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, he said: 'Whoever desires the kingdom of our sovereign intellect has exalted the prophets.' Muslim scholars have said: the Throne (kursī) is the sphere of the Law (falak al-nāmūs)...

The Throne (Arsh) is in the ninth sphere, and there is no doubt about its existence, for the verses and reports about it are without number and weight. He said in truth: 'His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth' (Quran 2:255), and 'He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne' (Quran 9:129). Abu al-Darr, may God be pleased with him, reported from the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, that he said: 'The seven heavens in relation to the Footstool (Kursi) are but like a ring thrown in a desert, and the superiority of the Throne over the Footstool is like the superiority of that desert over that ring.' That is, the Throne surpasses created things to such a degree that the Truth — Exalted and Majestic — made it the qibla of the people of spiritual stations, and it has been transmitted from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, that he said: There is no believer on earth who bows and prostrates himself but that his counterpart in the Throne also bows and prostrates, and the angels of that counterpart pray for that first believer and seek forgiveness for him. But when a believer on earth is occupied with sin and does not bow — at that moment the angels of that counterpart rebuke him until those believers are informed. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked about the speech: 'O You who reveal the mighty and conceal the ugly!' — and it is permissible for all creation whether seen or unseen to draw near to the Throne, though in truth its dimensions are such that the ninth sphere is but a limit beside it, and its depth no one but God the Exalted can measure. Its surface area is four hundred and seventy thousand and six hundred and sixty-two miles. The supreme sphere encompasses all the other spheres, and the spheres — some of them and others — and the terrestrial sphere together comprise thirteen spheres each encompassing the other. The most beautiful of forms is the spherical form, and for this reason the Exalted Truth — Glory and Majesty be His — created all things He mentioned and fashioned them in this form, as depicted here.

Verification of its station and precision of its aim: here in detail I wish to mention that this pure and generous thought — that the worlds of bodies should be encompassing — came about such that all bodies are divided into two divisions: one division is the simple bodies, which are the bodies of differing natures, and the other division is the compound bodies, that is to say, bodies of differing natures which are compounds. Among these are minerals, plants, and animals. One of the simples, which is a subdivision, consists of the elements — that is, earth, water, air, and fire — and another subdivision is the ethereal bodies together with the celestial spheres. The simple body, by its own nature and requirement, comes out spherical in form. The elements and ethereal bodies are spherical in shape, and it has come down that the earth likewise is capable of being spherical, though otherwise...

In that region (climate/zone), the arrangement of the stars is such that it resembles a desert plateau, and the mines appear in layers on the surface. The livelihoods of animals and humans depend upon it, and the springs of water flow there quickly, so that caravans draw water and it is as a vessel; and the material is not firmly fixed. Because when rising from the earth and ascending, one passes over the mountains and descends, moving and circling around.

And the concave (hollow) of its air — those same arrangements of the stars — completes a full circuit upon the earth, until it reaches that sphere of fire. All of the celestial spheres are encompassed within this form and arrangement, surrounding the earth entirely in its midst.

In the middle is the Earth; around it is the sphere of Water; around that is the sphere of Air; around that is the sphere of Fire; around that is the sphere of Mercury (Utarid); around that is the sphere of Venus (Zuhra); around that is the sphere of the Sun (Shams); around that is the sphere of Mars (Mirrikh); around that is the sphere of Jupiter (Mushtari); around that is the sphere of Saturn (Zuhal); around that is the sphere of the Fixed Stars; and beyond that is the outermost sphere, which appears beyond that circle, as has been mentioned.

From the detailed account mentioned above, it becomes clear that the stars rise from the East and set in the West — as is apparent. But the stars called 'Kanz' and the wandering ones face the spheres, not turning back, because the spheres are solid and not receptive to penetration or piercing. And since the simple spheres (al-aflak al-basita) are such, from them various effects proceed.

So it becomes known that the stars are embedded within the solid spheres, not floating freely within them, and the spheres encompass the Earth, surrounding it in their extent. The stars also extend in their lengths, and the movement of the spheres carries along the movement of the stars embedded within them — just as the movement of a millstone carries what is upon it. The stars are of two kinds: some are Planets (Sayyarat) and some are Fixed Stars (Thawaabit). The planets are seven, each moving upon its own sphere, level by level, and each of their movements produces effects.

The Twelfth Observation: Those who dwell in the heavens — all of them, without exception — are angels. An angel is a being endowed with life and rational speech, purified from the darkness of carnal impulses, passions, anger, and disobedience — things found, for example, among humans. God Most High has described them thus: 'They do not disobey God in what He commands them, but do what they are commanded.' They have no need of food or drink, they do not die, their nourishment is glorification and praise, their sanctification is exaltation, their rest is the remembrance of God Most High, and their joy is in worship. The creatures of the heavens differ in their forms and their ranks.

Know that the creation of angels was for the benefit and rectification of all created things. That angels exist in the celestial spheres is established; it is also confirmed by rational proof, for God Most High did not leave the spheres disordered and empty. Rather, He created within them various kinds of living beings, filled the air with birds, the dry land with beasts and wild animals, the mountains with solid creatures, and populated the darkness and dust — indeed, He created kinds of living beings and filled them with souls to overflowing, and for every spring, valley, and mine there are angels appointed. How then could the luminous, transparent spheres — the most refined of all God Most High's creations — be empty of angels?

The angels are of all kinds, and God Most High alone knows their true number, as He said: 'And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him.' It is reported from the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, in a well-known tradition that from the atoms of the universe there is not a single space the size of a hand's span but an angel is appointed over it. Not a single drop of rain descends without an angel being assigned to it. And upon the Throne and the Footstool, there is no spot, however small, that is not occupied by an angel engaged in worship — as is well established.

The Messenger of God — upon whom be the finest of blessings — declared: 'The most pleasant of fragrances and the truest of rights belong to…' Upon that place, this span [of heaven] exists, and upon it the angels are prostrate. The angels — not one type but of many kinds — serve [God] and draw apart from it. The Creator of the universe has described them from within [His knowledge], saying: 'We have no station save a known one, and verily we are ranged in ranks, and verily we give glory [to God].' It follows that some angels perform the prayer as Adam's community does, standing in straight rows, upright in posture, remaining standing in prayer before God.

And some angels are in a state of bowing (rukū') in their worship, never disdaining [to serve]. As the Lord of Glory declares: 'Those who are in His presence do not disdain to worship Him' — by this is meant the honor of nearness [to God].

Some angels are in prostration, and within [the context of] prostration it is permissible — indeed, in that state [it is required] — as the Word of God Most High is proof of this: 'And when We said to the angels: Prostrate yourselves before Adam, so they prostrated, except Iblis — he refused and was arrogant and was of the disbelievers' [Quran 2:34]. But from this standalone argument, what is meant is the shari'a meaning, and by 'angels' is meant all of them — that is, this is to be understood in that manner.

And some angels are seated, continuously engaged in praise and glorification — they are the angels of praise (hamd).

Story: Uwais al-Qarani — may God have mercy on him — is reported to have said: 'I shall worship in such a way that the angels in heaven will take note.' One night he would stand [in prayer] from the beginning until dawn, and another night he would remain in bowing (ruku') from the beginning until dawn, and another night he would remain in prostration (sujud) from the beginning until dawn.
The first night he would prostrate from dawn onward, spending the night entirely in worship.
