15. Daybahr, 16. Mihr, 17. Sorush, 18. Dosh, 19. Farvardin, 20. Bahram, 21. Ram, 22. Vad
23. Daydeen, 24. Deen, 25. Ard, 26. Ashnod, 27. Asman, 28. Zamiyad, 29. Marassfand
30. Anbaran. And Malakjar — meaning that for each of these days of the month, the one who acts in accordance with its corresponding celestial day, it brings about the favorable alignment. For example: Bahram corresponds to the second day of Aban month; the sixth day is Ard-bahisht; Shahrevar is the fourth day; Khordad is the fifth day; Morad is the sixth day; Zi is the eighth day; Azar is the ninth day; Aban is the tenth day; Tir is the thirteenth day; Zi is the eighteenth day; Mihr corresponds to the sixteenth day; Farvardin corresponds to the twenty-ninth day; and Zi Garm is the twenty-third day.

And Malakjar — whoever gives a name to the first [day] mentioned above, designating which foods, clothing, and customs are appropriate and ordained, and whoever acts accordingly — for the days that are favorable to his heart, let him mention those affairs that concern him regarding food and drink. And whoever carries out [the fast of] Amordad for those who observe it, the food and beverage designated for it, their soul will attain joy, and from the multitude of creation, no harm shall come to those who listen to it with sincerity. It has been said: those who observe it for the sake of its lords will attain goodness and the acquisition of otherworldly felicity. So let us mention the details of Malakjar one by one, in order that the complete state of each may become known. It is Nowruz — the first day — and it is said that God Almighty sends forth on that day to all the celestial spheres what He wills.

Anecdote: It is related that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Akks, may God be pleased with him, brought a gift to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, and it is said that there was halvah inside it, and this is the answer they gave.

The sweetness of joy: They first told of it, saying it was tremendous, and the messenger brought it. Thus those people who left their homeland were revived — some had died of plague and others from natural causes. God revealed, as stated in Surah Al-Baqarah: 'Have you not seen those who left their homes in thousands, fearing death? God said to them: Die! Then He restored them to life.' These people, it is said, were from the city of Dawur, and their story is well known; the name of that great land is Marmara — some say it is derived from the Names of God — and it is said that on the day of this gathering, 'O people of Dhann,' from morning one does not speak without a measure of gratitude as is written. And if the enemy approaches from any direction, and if the people of that place rise from sleep in the morning and make good acts of devotion — for example, if a king rises in the morning and sees his servant mounted on horseback with a falcon, and if seventy-nine warriors were gathered — these two, finding harmony, would come together for a great feast. The king would distribute among the common people gifts and rewards; and in the second category, those of his household and relatives would receive honors and gifts; and in the third category, distinguished persons would receive fine gifts and honors; and in the fourth category, his own children and descendants would receive all manner of kindness. In sum, in these five categories he would distribute gifts and honors generously to all, and after the worshippers had finished their duties.

...and their companions gathered together in festivity. Ordibehesht: The middle of spring, the first day is blessed. On the third day, by the order corresponding to the angel whose name matches Ordibehesht, there is a festival. This angel is appointed over fire and light, and through him the sick are healed of their illnesses.

Khordad: The last month of spring. On the sixth day of this month, according to the corresponding name of the angel below, a festival called Khordadgan is held in villages and towns. Khordad is the name of an angel responsible for the cultivation of plants and trees and the flowing of waters. He is appointed over these matters.

Mehr: The first month of autumn. On the sixteenth day of this month is the great festival of Mehraban. On the first day, Fereydun's light prevailed and conquered. In the middle of autumn, on the seventh day, it is a festival known as Mardad.

Shahrivar: The last month of summer. On the fourth day of this month, there is a festival known as Shahrivar. 

Tir: The first month of autumn. On the nineteenth day of this month, the festival of Tirgan is held in villages and towns, which is considered extremely blessed, because when Afrasiyab had conquered the lands of Iran, a truce was made and the lands of Iran were restored to peace.

Abān: The middle of autumn. On the third day of this month, the festival of Abanegan is held in villages. It is customary that people spread food for animals on that day. Birds such as eagles and vultures descend from the sky, and the animals eat from that food, and the people observe their behavior.

Āẕar: The last month of autumn. On the third day of this month, the festival of Āẕarjashn is held. People go to the fire temples, pay respects at the sanctuaries, and offer sacrifices. The affairs of the world and the interests of the realm are consulted on this day, and on this day various kinds of competitions are held.

The people of that region suffered greatly; they wore rough garments and their bodies were afflicted with ailments. The people complained and gathered, crying out against oppression, becoming wretched and lowly. Thus had this custom continued for many years in that land, until a king came and, seeing the situation, imposed a levy. With this levy sufficient wealth was gathered and ease was obtained, and another guardian of that place was appointed. It is said that whoever eats the citron there for a full year will be fortunate. On the eighth day, the tenth day, and the fifteenth day of that month, the king for the first time put on a magnificent robe and sat upon his throne. His chamberlains and heralds went out, and other kings and princes came to him. The kings came, and their followers arrived, and the king held counsel with them, saying: 'I too shall build great buildings, for the world is built up through great works, and the building of the world means governance and order.' He persuaded them of this. Bahman told the ancient story of which day of the month it was, that he had ordered Bahman-i Surkh and Bahman-i Sefid to gather all the animals, and each one, in its misery, came and recognized the other, and the image of the assembly was thus recorded. Bahman is the name of the angel who is the overseer of animals — Bahmazar Mazd — whose name in the old tradition means the angel whose name signifies the one appointed over the creatures of the earth, the tame animals, the wild ass, and all living creatures.

The Seventh Chapter
Since the third type [of reckoning] was not deemed sufficiently detailed, we contented ourselves with this much.

The Seventh Chapter: It is to be known that in general the Arabs, the Romans (Byzantines), and the Persians (Ajam) each have their own calendar. The Arab calendar is based on the lunar [year], which consists of twenty-nine days per month, reckoned by the shadow, totaling three hundred [and some] days. The Roman and Persian calendar is solar, and for this reason it consists of three hundred and sixty-five days — with a Kasri (fractional) portion remaining, making a slight difference between these two types of reckoning. As has been stated in the discourse on this: 'Thalthana sineen' — meaning, the Romans repeat [their cycle thus] — and 'Waradha wa ittasa'a' — meaning, the Arabs extend [their count] — and so it continues.

When the Sun comes to rest at the point of the equinox, it then moves on from there and continues until it returns to that [same] point, completing its circuit. This is called one solar year, and it is divided into four parts, each part called a season (fasl). Each season has its own qualities and characteristics, one differing from another. And if it were the case that summer followed winter at once, in a single moment, it would be a tremendous shock to the body, and the transition of the calendar from one extreme to the other would be sudden.

At the time of the vernal equinox, the days and nights become equal. As a result, at that moment equilibrium is achieved: the streams and rivers begin to flow, the waters in the fields become abundant, the moisture rises in the trees, the roots send up new shoots, the flowers blossom, the face of the earth is covered with fresh vegetation, the air becomes temperate, the creatures are renewed, the animals and birds and livestock appear upon the mountains — all is fresh and alive.

The life of the people of that time is pleasant, and joy appears on the face of the earth — the world is like a beautiful young maiden. It becomes orderly, and when the sun enters Gemini, spring becomes complete. And when it reaches the point of Cancer, summer begins — it is as the skilled farmer knows: days reach their greatest length and nights their shortest. The animals grow strong and the waters warm; the trees grow lush and the birds sing, pouring forth melodies. The edges of the land become filled with sounds and voices, and humans and other creatures enjoy abundant life. The world reaches its perfection and beauty, and the earth is covered in greenery. When the sun reaches the end of Leo, summer is complete. When it reaches the point of Libra, the autumnal equinox occurs, and day and night become equal. The plants and trees begin to wither, and the cold winds arrive. The waters diminish and all kinds of vegetation declines. People and animals become still, and insects retreat. Birds migrate to warmer lands, and people begin to think of shelter. When the sun enters Sagittarius, autumn is complete. When it reaches the point of Capricorn, the winter solstice occurs — days are at their shortest and nights at their longest. The cold arrives, people are freed from agricultural labor, and they remain in their homes eating and drinking — whereas in summer people toil in hardship, in winter they rest. As the Arabs say: 'In summer they sweat in the fields, in winter they huddle from the cold.'

The Volkhash region, with its wild and naked spirits, and the animals that dwell there numbering nine hundred thousand in the world — all those creatures gathered together, the animals assembled side by side, approaching one another in that vicinity. When the appointed time draws near, the world is as though the final hour approaches, and the name of God is praised, and he returns to his former state as before, until it reaches [its limit].

Chapter Eight: Concerning the wonders related to certain persons — rather, as some sages have said, whenever God Almighty willed, He sent through one of His prophets strange miracles, so that the truth might be manifested and the testimony of Divine Unity made clear to all. The purpose behind each of them was this: that the prophet would come and fulfill that very purpose through which the proof was established — that a prophet had arrived. The first thousand years belonged to Abu al-Bashar Adam, upon him be the peace and blessings of God. The second thousand belonged to the great ones. The third thousand belonged to Ibrahim (Abraham), the Friend of God, upon him be the blessings of God. The fourth thousand belonged to Musa (Moses), the Speaker with God, upon him be the blessings of God. The fifth thousand belonged to Sulayman (Solomon) and Dawud (David), upon them be peace. The sixth thousand belonged to 'Isa (Jesus), the Spirit of God, upon him be the blessings of God. And the seventh thousand belongs to the Seal of the Prophets and Master of Saints, Muhammad, the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him — with whom prophethood was sealed, and with whom the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) finds its completion. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may God be pleased with him, reports from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that: 'The world is but a week among the weeks of the Hereafter — seven parts. And at the head of each sign from the sending of our Prophet, one appeared who raised the banners of religion: over the first, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may his memory be sanctified; over the second, Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him; over the third, Ahmad ibn [Hanbal/Kunjurih], may his memory be sanctified.'

And the fourth is Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib al-Baqillani, and the fifth is Abu Hamid Muhammad al-Ghazali, and likewise the sixth is Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Umar al-Razi, may God be pleased with them all — meaning that in the world, from every century, after the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him) and after his devotion, from a hundred years onward, one who raises the banners of outward knowledge would appear. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz appeared in the second hundred; Imam al-Shafi'i appeared in the third hundred; Ahmad ibn Hanbal appeared in the fourth hundred; Abu Bakr al-Baqillani appeared in the fifth hundred; Imam Muhammad al-Ghazali appeared in the sixth hundred; Imam Muhammad al-Razi appeared in the seventh hundred — may God have mercy on them all.

From Anas ibn Malik: Whoever God grants a life of forty years, God the Most High will protect him from various afflictions, among them leprosy, vitiligo, and madness. Whoever God grants fifty years, God will lighten his account on the Day of Judgment. Whoever God grants sixty years, God will grant him repentance and turning back to Him. Whoever God grants seventy years, the inhabitants of heaven and earth will count him among the blessed. Whoever God grants eighty years, his good deeds will be recorded and his intercession accepted. Whoever God grants ninety years, God will forgive his sins and he will be called a captive upon the earth, and he shall intercede for the people of his household.

From the one whom God is pleased with — it is said that such a person of good long life will be protected from various afflictions: one from severance, one from certain harms, one from madness, and will attain wholeness. As for the one whom God grants a long life and who returns to God with a pure heart — whoever lives long enough will attain their reward. As for the one whom God grants eighty years of life, God Most High will preserve them from all sins and grant them treasures.

Such a person — if a servant of God the Most High commits sins, and God Most High so wills, his intercession will be accepted, and through him people will be granted mercy and forgiveness. The revolutions of the celestial spheres manifest wondrous events in the world, and strange living creatures of wondrous forms are born. Rare minerals, trees, and plants come into being in regions of the world. Prosperous lands fall to ruin; seas overturn other seas; mountains are leveled flat. All of this comes to pass: 'Such is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.' This is what the Tablet of the Sublime Pen records.

It is related — and God the Eternal knows best — a story: Among the Children of Israel there was a righteous young man. The elders gathered and brought that young man before the king, saying: 'He has surpassed us. Either kill him or banish him.' The king, upon seeing the young man in this state, fell into thought. Then Khidr came and said to the young man: 'The king wishes to see you — he desires to meet you — otherwise he will have you killed.' Khidr came to him and said: 'Go to the king.' The young man went to the king, and the king said: 'Show me something of Khidr's station, of a degree I have not seen before.' And Khidr showed him many wonders. Then it occurred to him to take him to a land on a great journey. I saw a great city and many people going and coming; and in the end, of all the people of that city, I found not a single one remaining. I said: 'I have reached this ancient city. I do not know who built it — even my fathers' fathers, for five hundred years, nothing of it remains.' I found there an old man and asked him: 'How did this city come to ruin?' He said: 'From that time onward.' I walked on and found another city that had been built — it too was now in ruins.'

From my father I also heard this: after traveling five hundred leagues, I encountered a calamity and mishap there. While catching fish I said, 'What a time has come,' and the people answered, 'The sea is right here,' and I said, 'I found it.' My father also heard from his fathers: after traveling five hundred leagues through those lands, I encountered a dry place, I saw a man coming to cut grass, I said, 'Is this place nearby or far?' He said, 'It is close.' And from my father I heard: after five hundred leagues from those lands, I encountered there an incomparable idol of wondrous form and contrivance. I said, 'When was this made?' They replied, 'It was made from ancient times.' And our fathers also asked about this: after five hundred leagues beyond that, I encountered a city. I asked an elder of that city, 'When was this city founded?' He said, 'It is very ancient, we do not know when it was built, nor do our fathers know; a certain wise governor came and thought: this world is subject to change, the abode of transience is not the abode of permanence, the true abode is the hereafter.' I said to myself, 'I will abandon kingship and become the companion of this man.' He said, 'You cannot be my companion, but accompany this young man, that will be better for you.' But indeed, from among the most wondrous things, a great personage arrived, and after coming he would take various forms and shapes, appearing in one image after another — and in truth, whoever looks upon this person has never seen him in any single form.'

For a human being — whether infant, child, young person, adolescent, adult, mature, or old — the transformations and changes are not exclusive to humankind, but encompass all animals as well. This is the true state of affairs. Those who are heedless of this reality and do not reflect upon it will eventually come to recognize — after all these successive changes — that the transfer to the afterlife is inevitable.

The Year of the Mouse: When the Year of the Mouse begins, it is characterized by abundance, pleasantness, and pride. Within it, rain and moisture are plentiful, hunting is diminished, and fruits and produce are abundant. However, grain becomes scarce. In truth, rulers will experience grief and distress, distances will feel far, and mice will proliferate greatly. People in cities should beware. But one who is born in this cycle will come into existence extremely clever and sickly, yet their words will be accepted among the great. In the middle of the year, signs of glory appear. They will be virtuous in appearance but unreliable in character. Toward the end of the year, those born will be deceitful, ill-tempered, and gloomy.

The Second Year, called the Year of the Ox: When the Year of the Ox begins, illness and disease spread greatly, and there are disruptions. But war and turmoil in the world will be repelled, rulers will gain respect and fame. People will incline toward justice, and there will be shortages of food and livestock in two regions. Those born in this cycle toward the end will be prosperous. Those born in the middle of the year will be good, fortunate, and blessed with many followers. Those born at the end of the year will be prosperous but lacking in generosity.

The Third Year, called the Year of the Leopard: When the Year of the Leopard comes, anger, vengeance, death of animals, and oppression of people occur. Injustice intensifies, rebellions break out in cities, earthquakes strike, and calamities befall some regions at the beginning of the year. One born in this cycle will be brave, noble-spirited, handsome in appearance, and speak well. Those born in the middle of the year will be...

...beautiful, fond of hunting, and abundantly provided with sustenance, and those born at the end of this year will be complete in grace.

The second sign: they call it the Year of the Rabbit. Because it is the Year of the Rabbit, work and blessings and fruits will be plentiful, and living conditions will be good. If plague and epidemic occur in the cities, the cold will be sharp; and in spring and in the season of pestilence, disturbances will arise in the western regions, and rains will fall, and rumors will be plentiful. One born when Jupiter is in Aries in this year will be hasty and faithless and untrustworthy of word; one born in the middle of the year will be sweet of tongue; one born at the end of the year will be talkative but beneficial.

The fifth sign: they call it the Year of the Dragon. Because it is the Year of the Dragon, strife and turmoil will be plentiful; rain and snow will fall little, and the cold of trees will be severe, bringing blight, and provisions will be firm, and there will be affliction. One born when Jupiter is in Aries in this year will be of bad disposition and shameless, a trouble-maker, an enemy of secrets, suited for base company.

The sixth sign: they call it the Year of the Snake. Because it is the Year of the Snake, there will be drought and little fruit; provisions will be firm, and the people will be in fear; plague will occur, and food and wages will be scarce, and people will be in want. One born when Jupiter is in Aries in this year will be quiet, dominant, of good intellect, gentle, and of pleasant character; he will speak little; one born in the middle of the year will be of bad nature and harboring malice; one born at the end of the year will be foul of speech and faithless.

The seventh sign: they call it the Year of the Horse. Because it is the Year of the Horse, in the direction of Turkestan there will be war and strife in two places, and provisions will be firm...

Among the animals, angels, fruits, and heavenly bodies: one born under this [sign] will be rarely encountered by death in infancy. Many events will occur in spring, and the cold will be harsh. One born under the red [Mars] will grow up robust and the ruler's strife will be accepted, and the middle of the year will bring forth a world of beauty and fine appearance. One born at the year's end will be of bad temperament and melancholy, growing up with harshness and difficulty — know that when the ship of the year arrives, it brings hardship — and such a person will find no companions of their kind, their affairs will be firm and ordered, and they will be blessed with many good deeds; fear and strife will arise, and powerful, jealous, ambitious souls will bring hardship. One born under the red [Mars] in that ascendant will be a loyal friend, fair-faced, of graceful form, and generous in sustenance. They will be a good person and learned, but will not benefit from the learned, and one born in the middle of the year will be of fine appearance and of good conduct; one born at the year's end will be weak, often ill, and without strength. Know that the name of this year is 'Sal-i Mun' — in it, the kings' thrones will be shaken and the weak will be many. Oppression will increase, thieves and those who cut off [roads] will be plentiful, and kings will make war and their rule will be firm, though fear of oppression will exist. One born under the red [Mars] in that ascendant will grow up learned, refined, virtuous, and of good character, though in the middle of the year envious; and one born at the year's end will be loyal in nature. Know that the name of this year is 'Sal-i Murgh' — in it, spring will be precious and the cold will be fierce, and sunshine will be scarce. One born under the red [Mars] in that ascendant will earn [a living] but their earnings will be wasted and dissipated, gathering nothing, and the middle of the year will bring forth abundance. And [they will be] numerous in enemies; at the year's end one born will pursue vengeance and [show] compassion.

The eleventh year is called the Year of the Ox. They say: when the Year of the Ox comes, floods will be severe, dust storms will rise, and fruits will be scarce. Animals will fall ill, and those born therein will be of good character and disposition. Those born in the middle of the year will be brave warriors, while those born at the end of the year will be ignorant and gluttons.

The twelfth year is called the Year of the Pig. They say: when the Year of the Pig comes, in that year locusts and calamities will fall upon the land, horses and plagues will multiply, foodstuffs will be spoiled, and the four limbs will suffer affliction. Diseases will be widespread, the roads will be long and arduous, and among the rulers there will be disagreement and conflict. Wolves and wild animals will increase greatly, the East will suffer destruction, and the people will be scattered and displaced, their affairs falling into disorder. Those born in this year under this cycle will be self-reliant, considering themselves wise, benefiting only themselves and not others, passing their time in their own company. Those born in the middle of the year will be brave and skilled in battle, while those born at the end of the year will be of good nature.

And another method: the divination of victor and vanquished (ghālib and maghlūb) is as follows — as the philosopher Aristotle composed for Alexander the Greek: when this book was compiled and made famous through Alexander, he used it to elevate and distinguish the noble from the base, raising some and humbling others, so that whoever intended to go to a province and undertake a campaign would reckon through this method whether he himself would be dominant in the calculation; if he came out dominant, he would proceed; if not, he would refrain and not send his commanders, for the method of this calculation is as follows:

Take the names of the two persons, add up the numerical values of the letters of each name together, then cast out nines repeatedly — that is, divide by nine and look at the remainder. For example, if one name gives three and the other gives eight, look at the table: eight is the victor and three is the vanquished. Thus the one whose name yields eight is the winner and the one whose name yields three is the loser.

Some authorities hold that what is to be counted is the given name; others hold that the surname, title (laqab), and honorific (kunya) and tribal affiliation (nisba) are all to be reckoned, and that what is well-known and established among people of the same city should be used. If the remainders of the two persons' names are equal, the one whose remainder is the larger is judged the victor. But some have said this is not always so: they say the one with the larger number is judged the winner, while others say that if both are equal, whichever of the two is the more fortunate, that one will prevail. And if one of them is a man of the sword (ṣāḥib sayf) and the other a man of the pen (ṣāḥib qalam), the man of the sword is judged the victor and the man of the pen is judged the loser. This method is considered reliable and well-tested for matters of battle, siege, and military campaigns, and its outcome is accepted among scholars.

But that omen on the left side of the table — know that the person's wish from it will come to good, and it is a fortunate omen.

And let it be known: in the view of the pillars of this [science], as Salava Akhsar — may Imad al-Din be remembered — one and the same thing, and it becomes known therein.

And know that regarding the agricultural rules related to omens, we will explain some of them. As some books have written and others have mentioned: to know when rain will fall or when leaves will appear, if you wish to know which month to plant — that is, to learn the nature of that planting — on the twenty-eighth day of the month of August, after sunset until dawn, look toward the middle of the sky in the northwest direction. If clouds appear there, rain will fall in the middle of the coming months and hail will come to the lowlands. If there are no clouds there, no rain will fall in the middle of the coming months. If the clouds are on the edge of the eye of the sky, and if the clouds appear from the southwest or are level, rain will come in the front part of the eye of the sky. If clouds appear at midnight, rain will come in the latter part of the eye of the sky. If clouds appear from the east before dawn, abundant rain will come throughout the eye of the sky. If the clouds are thick, much rain will fall; if the clouds are thin, little rain will fall. If the clouds fill the entire sky with a blue-gray color, rain will fall throughout the entire eye of the sky. If the clouds are in patches, rain will fall here and there. And know that the twenty-eighth day of August that we have mentioned indicates the nature of the rainfall in the eye of the sky [i.e., the coming season].

It is also reported among the wonders: that during the time of teething in children, the influence of the planets at the hour of birth determines the governance of the four temperaments thereafter — for the newborn body is moist and quickly affected, and its primary nourishment...

When four years have passed, Mercury becomes dominant over the person along with those ten, and their understanding, sciences, crafts, and apparent capacities for learning and discernment grow stronger. The foundations of morals and the particular characteristics of actions that arise from them are established through instruction, proper conduct, and wisdom. After completing four full stages, one comes under the dominion of Venus from the age of fourteen, during which there arise inclinations toward commerce, movement, pleasure, festivity, love, affection, attention, sexual union, and the stirring of desire. After that, the Sun becomes dominant over them through age twenty-nine, granting nobility, self-mastery, strength, dignity, purity of soul, and the capacity for noble actions and transitions. After that, Mars becomes dominant through age thirty-five, bringing forth anxieties about livelihood, concern for family, greed, and length of ambition — as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'When the son of Adam grows old, two things increase in him: greed and length of hope.' After that, Jupiter becomes dominant through age forty-eight, during which one becomes free from heavy labors, attaining good circumstances, remembrance of God, seeking noble company, and inclining toward earning merit. After that, Saturn becomes dominant over the final part of life, and there appear coldness, laziness, slowness of movement, hastiness of error, and decline. Moreover, the time of one's birth and what fortune is near at the moment of birth — if it coincides with a great benefic star's period — then the person's wealth, power, and prominence become manifest at that time. This is why some people's fortune appears in youth, others' in middle age, others' manifest late, and for some it appears before old age.

Some of them bring death, and from the wonders of forgiveness, one listens to the subtleties. The author begins his discourse, and from the rarities mentioned nearby, I shall now mention: The Third Treatise. By 'the lower realms' is meant what occupies the spheres — that is, the elements, the three kingdoms of nature, thunder and lightning, meteorological phenomena, the rainbow, and other such occurrences that are transient, swift in their elemental nature, and swift to pass. These encompass all of them. Consider first, under the First Observation, the elements — which are divided into two chapters. Chapter One: On the True Nature of the Elements. The fundamental element from which they originate is water, and the primary elements are four: hot, cold, moist, and dry. Each pair combines: fire is hot and dry, air is hot and moist, water is cold and moist, and earth is cold and dry. These four are what are called 'elements.' The three kingdoms — plants, minerals, and animals — are their compounds, produced by combination according to the relational compound. Their compounds according to relation, and to elaborate further: the compounds formed from their combinations by relational composition are what they call 'elements,' brought to equilibrium through the most perfect arrangement. In absolute terms — meaning that fire in its entirety moves upward by nature of its lightness toward the first, air does so for the reason of levity in its absolute sense, earth downward for the reason of gravity absolutely, and the concavity of the sphere of fire, the convexity of the sphere of air, the concavity of the sphere of air, the convexity of the sphere of earth, the concavity of the sphere of water — these are the proper places of the elements. The quality by which elements become moderate is that two of the qualities are made median: each element shares one quality with its neighbor in agreement and differs from it in the other quality.

Neighbors differ in consideration such that fire does not mix with its neighbors, for each of the two is adjacent, and air and water are neighbors with fire because each of them is also a neighbor in nature. And the neighbors of water also include coldness and moisture, which does not mix with fire's neighbors. The wisdom of the Almighty ordained this: that the absolutely light is closest to the celestial sphere, and the absolutely heavy is farthest from it, and air and water, whose lightness and heaviness are relative, remain between the sphere and the earth, so that the lighter inclines toward the sphere and the heavier toward earth.

Second Chapter: On the transformation of elements into one another. Know that elements transform into one another because their forms differ while their substance is the same. But that transformation which occurs between water and earth: for example, in Azerbaijan there is a spring whose water, when the local people take it and pour it into molds, turns to stone. And there is another spring: whoever drinks from it turns to stone. Just as, for instance, the Aksitata stone, when placed in water, dissolves. As for the transformation between air and water: for example, on mountain peaks, sometimes through the agency of air, vapor transforms into rain and falls inside a vessel or outside it, and the air that is outside turns like musk-like water, and when it transforms, if the sun's heat reaches the water collected in a vessel, it becomes vapor and becomes air. As for the transformation between fire and air...

Air becomes fire — when the blacksmith blows into the bellows, the compressed air shoots out and continuously strikes, so the air that accompanies the heat becomes like fire, as copper and water rush together to ignite it, and the fire causes the air next to it to become so transformed that it is like the wick of a lamp: when the wick of a lamp is kindled by fire, it reveals the secret — for the air mixed with it, from the mingling of the smoky particles, turns dark and takes on the nature of fire, and the air becomes part of the fire. In what follows there are two chapters, Chapter One:

The Second Consideration: Concerning the Sphere of Fire and What Lies Within It

The reality of fire is this: the sphere of pure simple fire is of such a color that, try as you might, you cannot see it — just as the blacksmith's bellows, when pressed and blown into sufficiently, if you were to look, you would see something like a concave mirror of catastrophe. The fire that is in the concave surface of the celestial sphere — if it were visible and one could see it, it would obstruct the vision of the world's destruction. And in that warm, sweet place, because it is a simple body mixed with air, it is so. It is through the perfect wisdom of God Most High that He made fire in the concave surface of the celestial sphere, so that its heat would burn the thick smoke rising up, and only a very small, refined part would remain, and the upper air would remain pure and clear. And from it He created the sphere of intense cold, so that the intensity of the heat of fire would be repelled, and living things — animals and plants — could exist thereby. Such is the wonder of the craft of God Most High: dark, dense, and opaque matter — and yet pure fire appears from it, and it is subtle. It is among the wonders of His craft that green wood produces fire, as He says: 'He who made for you from the green tree fire, and behold, you kindle from it.' There are two trees: one is the morj and the other is the ghafar. One produces fire when rubbed with the other, as reported by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abkalas, may God be pleased with them both.

There is no tree so great that its fire does not rise up—whatever passes by is consumed in its blaze, and the sparks fly out like shooting stars and fall as embers. Among the wonders of the power of the Most High—glory be to Him—is that He separated the Children of Israel from the fire, so the fire burned on every side around them yet did not touch them. And the Most High God, in the perfection of His power, gave to fire a force that destroys bodies, consuming the wicked and the sinners. It burns through iron, steel, and lead, and is useful to people in many necessary ways. The Most High God arranged things so that fire provides travelers with their provisions for the road, producing food where none existed, as He said: 'We made it a reminder and a provision for travelers—so glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.' Among the wonders of God's creation: it is told that a righteous man once put on a garment and it appeared to him like fruit; at harvest and gathering time, this would call the attention of the poor and draw their hearts near. The leaves that fell, and the gleaning left in the field, and what was spread about from threshing—that which fell outside belonged to the poor, and the tithe was their right. That righteous man kept his word and fulfilled his obligations, and his enemies were laid low. His innermost heart was hidden—he endured, until at last God Most High fulfilled: 'We tested them as We tested the Companions of the Garden.' Among the wonders of God's creation—and I will relate something concerning a small body, though the nature of fire is refined: however small the spark, it spreads and grows. And among its wonders—it is established by verified accounts—observe: in the space of twelve nights it burned through the camels and consumed many of them; and some who looked on from outside could see the smoke but were not harmed by it. The Most High God sent an angel, and the angel dug a pit and buried the fire there, and the people saw the smoke rise. Second Chapter: On shooting stars, on comets, and on all [that follows].

...ascending from the smoke, that is, this shooting star rises up — each one that reaches [a certain height] is like a fragment breaking off. When that first smoke, which is connected to the earth, becomes attached and if it is fine and subtle, it ignites and thereafter the fire transforms within it, nourishing [what it encounters], so that it becomes invisible — meaning it disappears from sight. The star is extinguished but it is not truly extinguished; rather, in truth it has been transformed into fire. What people call 'shooting stars' are this: even though outwardly it appears that the star has been extinguished like a flame blown out, yet the density [of the smoke] — after the thick [part] has burned away — remains to a degree, like a reddish-black [glow] visible from afar. And creatures resembling dragons, columns, and long shapes in various forms become visible to common people, [who say] 'A comet appeared in the sky, [which is] a sign of the Day of Resurrection.' If that ascending smoke is connected to the earth and [the fire] reaches [it], the fire ignites and blazes, and as it burns through the earth [the smoke] condenses. Like a candle whose wick is extinguished [but whose wax remains], the smoke returns again and again to the place where it was extinguished, reigniting. So when a fire or this smoke returns repeatedly and appears at ground level, people call it a 'will-o'-the-wisp' or marsh fire — 'swamp lights' as common folk say — visible for several days. If one asks for the Quranic proof: In Surah al-Saffat [37:6-7]: 'Indeed We have adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of stars, and as a protection against every rebellious devil.' And in Surah al-Mulk [67:5]: 'And We have certainly beautified the lowest heaven with stars...'

"And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps, and We have made them missiles to drive away the devils" [Qur'an 67:5]. The commentators and scholars of exegesis have said in explanation of this: the meaning of 'missiles' is not that the stars themselves move — rather, it is as if a piece is broken off from a star and hurled. Thus it does not conflict with what has been established, for the Glorious Qur'an explicitly states this, contrary to what the philosophers say. What the philosophers mention has no real effect upon the devils. If it be asked: was the meteor ('shihab') not [known] before the Messenger of God, peace be upon him — [the answer is that] after his birth, those devils who used to eavesdrop on the heavens were prevented from doing so, and a smoky sphere of fire was sent to drive them away and scatter them. This is the sound position: the meaning of 'shihab' is that it is directed toward the devil, not that it is the Messenger of God, peace be upon him. It occurred after his birth — that is to say, the meteor is hurled at the devil from the stars. This occurred afterwards — that is, the fiery smoky sphere was sent to scatter and drive them away. The occurrence of the meteor before that time does not prevent this [interpretation].

The Third Discussion — concerning the sphere of air.

And this contains a first section. The First Section: On the true nature of air. Air is a simple, transparent body — that is, it has no color. The convex surface of the sphere of air is tangent to the concave surface of the lunar sphere. Air is naturally in motion, continuously moving and flowing — it is not naturally at rest; wind is merely air in motion. It is said that air near the earth is divided into three parts:

The First Part is that which is contiguous with the celestial sphere, rotating perpetually in continuous revolution.

And the speed of its motion is like fire, and at the utmost degree of heat in the sphere it diminishes somewhat in motion, and its heat decreases so that cold predominates and the cold wind blows.

The second layer is that of Venus, and in it the season and the cold wind and its rays strike back from the earth, and so the air that is reflected becomes temperate, and if it reaches equilibrium the cold dominates there.

The cold air increases more near the North Pole, and in the first regions six months of the year the air is so cold that the summer fills with darkness and cold, and the animals and plants there barely survive — indeed, most of them lack color, and the highest mountains there are only a few arm-spans in extent.

When these elements transform, things such as light and darkness, vapor and water — namely fog — and smoke, chill, rainbows, clouds, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, hail, snowstorms, hoarfrost, sleet, shooting stars, and halos come to be. Some of these occur in the upper air, as we have mentioned, and some occur near the surface of the earth.

Section Two: On clouds and rain. In brief, the scholars say: when the subtle parts rising from the earth follow the sun and are called vapor, and when these vapors strike the earth following the sun, the subtle parts rise up and are called vapor. When these vapors ascend, they are not free of moisture. If they reach the surface and the vapor and smoke reach the surface of the earth, and the cold is not strong enough to keep them aloft, they gather and become clouds, and from them raindrops descend, as follows...

When vapors rise up and go toward their region and descend from there, the droplets that fall are called rain. If the cold in the atmosphere is very strong and affects the cloud, those droplets while still within the cloud become solid (freeze), and if they fall as chunks they are called hail. If they accumulate and gather more, growing in the cold of the atmosphere, and then separate from the cloud by a certain measure, they become hail (large hail). If the cloud reaches close to the earth with only a little distance and settles near the ground — this is what they call dew (nida). If it descends as a fine, thin mist without the watery parts being frozen, it falls like a surface moisture, which is called dew (shabnam). If the watery parts descend frozen, that is called frost (saqi'), which is also called rime.

Compared to fine rain, thin dew is analogous — indeed, clouds arise entirely from the condensation of air due to intense cold. Imam al-Razi has said that most of the aforementioned phenomena arise from vapor, and sometimes due to the reduction (of heat) the condensation of matter occurs. The Most High God, in His perfect grace, has appointed angels over every rain and flood that pours down, directing them toward the lands that need water, so that the life of lands and people is sustained. Scholars of experience have said that in every place that forty days pass without rain, plants wither and animals perish — but the more correct view is this:

This is the Third Chapter: Know that the philosophers say that the sound of thunder is a wave through the air, just as waves form on water. When the water is still (calm), waves appear, but the heavy parts of the water are slow in movement.

When smoke ascends and reaches the cold layer, either its heat becomes still — in which case it descends and the spring clouds, having been cooled, acquire coldness — or it disperses downward, and the air below becomes turbulent and moves, such that it passes through. When the heat is not stilled and the sphere of fire draws it upward, that which moves does so with the circular motion of the celestial sphere, and by reason of this, it is brought downward; thus the air becomes turbulent and agitated, and passes through, meeting with the clouds. It then becomes heated, and since it moves with the motion of the sphere, it dissolves within the sphere's parts, and moves no longer; thus it passes through — either the air filled with clouds becomes turbulent and moves downward with a general thrust, and the turbulence spreads therein, and the air that is in it becomes turbulent again and moves, and passes through — or the cloud is expelled from one side toward another, and from that expulsion arises motion, and the air, being obligated by that, turns about, spinning from one side and penetrating the other, and the air itself, in its vicinity, sets the surrounding air in motion by its agitation; or, being brought down by its own nature, the descending air is repelled upward, and by this the air becomes turbulent and moves — hence the winds: they arise because of the excess of cold, and wherever they turn back, meeting the cold layer and encountering clouds, the clouds are struck, and that which was ascending is repelled and a thing becomes of it — such is the state of it, and it remains dry. The reason for this is that the great clouds act as a veil and screen, and the cold prevails; but some oppose it, and from their mixing arises the cause that prevents the beloved thing from reaching, and the causes of our misfortunes arise. Whoever wishes to understand this, let him consider: it lifts it up, it turns it about, and it brings it back around.

Around the palace of Ghaljan, winds arise and the beneficial breezes blow there; the poisonous winds (samum) have been seen.
The burning meteor falls, and from it the great fiery forms descend, making the poisonous wind appear before the eyes.
The shooting star (shihab) passes through the air, and by its passage the intense heat is extinguished and the angels record.
There are two kinds of thunderbolts: the first is a mercy and sustenance, and the second is of four or seven grades.
One type is of the dispersed kind, scattering and striking, and the lightning destroys and annihilates.
Both types occur at sea, and the thunderbolt descends, and the angels of the higher realm receive them.
The four winds: the North Wind (Shamal) — its starting point is from where the sun sets in the north, going to its setting.
The South Wind (Janub) — its starting point is from where the sun rises in the south going to its setting; the East Wind (Saba) — its starting point is from where the sun rises going to its setting.
The West Wind (Dabur) — its starting point is likewise from where the sun sets to where it sets.
The northern regions lie under the dominion of clouds, and in that country snow covers the land.
In those climes there are snows, rains, and floods, and in that country there are vast deserts.
The mountains are as numerous as the fires there; from the south, great mountains rise one after another.
From below those mountains, the herbs and plants grow, cultivated and beneficial.
The pure water flows from it, preserving health, and the purest air keeps the constitution sound.
In every land where the north and south winds blow together, the animals and plants grow in abundance.
Where the air is sparse, life is weak and thin; the Arab north wind blows away the poisonous miasmas.
It drives away diseases, brings rain, pours down blessings, clears the air, and brings coldness and freshness.

The south wind (al-janub) is hot and moist, for it comes from the direction of the equator, and its moisture is great, because it passes over the sea, and always being distant, in that region it is as much as is necessary.

It is necessarily hot and moist; it softens things and makes a complete person (i.e., those it reaches) weary and drowsy, and it opens the mouth wide. In particular, it weakens hearing and sight and causes the eyes to water, and creates laziness and much sleepiness.

Children born in that region tend to be gentle in disposition, and passing through [those conditions], water placed over it becomes cold, and cold water placed over it becomes warm. The northwest wind —

In this state, the peoples of the west find the south wind objectionable and praiseworthy [i.e., mixed in character]; it brings rain clouds and gives rain, sending the birds of passage on their way.

Chapter Four: On thunder and lightning in the sky — the angel who controls lightning strikes with measure, as the sages say:
When the sun heats the surface of the water, the water particles rise up — this is called vapor (bukhār). And when the sun heats the surface of the earth, the earth particles rise — this is called smoke (dukhān). The totality of these particles comes together, and the fine particles mix and rise together until they reach the freezing zone (Zamharīr). If the parts of the cloud condense and are retained within the cloud, they become imprisoned therein...

After that, the smoke moves upward, and since the heat has been applied to it, it is discharged all at once from the earthly elements that have gathered together. When the heat is dissipated and separation from the watery particles occurs, in either case, the movement of those golden sparks causes a rubbing and friction. From that, a sound emerges — that is thunder. And if the smoke and the clouds form a firm wall together, a mighty roar comes from it, which is what appears from the compression — if it is subtle, it bounces off and becomes lightning. And if there are earthly, pitch-like, sulfurous elements in it that catch fire, they ignite piece by piece, burning here and there in a straight line — that is what is called a thunderbolt, that is to say, yıldırım [lightning bolt]. If it is asked why lightning and thunderbolts strike more frequently in summer than they are found in winter: it is because the ascent of vapors, smoke, and earthly and sulfurous elements through the influence of the sun is greater in summer, and the earthly moisture is more concentrated. For this reason, they are found more often in summer and rarely in winter, unless in winter the cold has intensified greatly. Thunder and lightning are rare in cold regions, because the cold repels the vapors and converts them into water. As for the thunderbolt (yıldırım): its special property is that it melts iron, destroys tall trees, melts gold and silver inside purses, but does no harm to the purse itself. Anecdote: It is related thus — a young man's body was struck by a thunderbolt and fell from his horse. The body of the young man who had fallen was examined, and since the heat of the thunderbolt had dispersed — and as for the thunderbolt, when there is thunder and lightning, a person recites this supplication and story: 'O God, among those who fear the thunder...'

The angels of Hanifa, in a great multitude — if that be so, the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, prayed earnestly: 'O God, O God, do not destroy us in Your wrath, and do not ruin us with Your punishment; grant us pardon before that.' And in that land there is a marvel: its waters, when people drink of them, those who drink become of great physical stature but small of mind, while those who are great in intellect become [physically] large in circumstance.

A Story — Narrated by Sheikh Abu Ali ibn Sina:

He related that once in a certain place, a fragment of a meteor fell and two grayish-blue [stones or pieces] were separated from it. It rolled and struck the earth, and a man went and dug it up and lifted it. The Sultan Muhammad sent for it and commanded a man to bring it and have it carried. Many people tried to lift it and were unable. The swords and blades came to cut it but were themselves blunted. Swords were brought to strike it but Sheikh Abu Ali's companions — some of them — tried one after another, and still it would not move. The thunder and lightning came upon it; [nevertheless] forgiveness appeared [in the matter]. For the intercession [of thunder]: when thunder's roar reaches the air, a great compression occurs — it falls upon the small [fragments] and makes a sound. They looked and found it had contracted. 'Why?' [they asked.] 'Because the sound of the thunder reaches the air and compresses it.' And from that high air a voice like thunder comes asking 'Who are you?' — if there be such a thing — then afterward, like a treasure of lightning striking rapidly, it descends and opens. It then falls and rolls, and whoever tries to move it [further] from that place or remove it, let him not be prevented.

Chapter Five: On rainbows (qaws quzah), that is, on the colored bands that appear in clouds, and on smoke.

It is established that the sole cause of this phenomenon is as follows: When clouds settle and come to rest, the small water droplets within them become transparent and face one another, arranged in sequence one after another. When they are aligned in this way with small mirror-like surfaces, they receive and reflect light. The dark body of the celestial sphere, which holds its natural moisture, strikes against these water droplets and, reaching the dark body, forms a circle. Because those water droplets, upon reaching the dark body, act like small mirrors in repeated reflection, they show the shape of what faces them — just as a small curved mirror does not show the full shape but shows only a portion. This is how the arc appears. If it is asked: when it moves, how does the image form in those small parts? — the answer is that the fine droplets are very dense and closely packed, facing the dark body opposite. The two water-particle layers settle and consolidate, and if they are unable to settle firmly, the dark body facing them causes the light to pass through, yielding a kind of transparency, like crystal facing the dark body. This is how the arc appears. It is also established that when two clouds of the described quality meet, rubbing against each other, the large arc appears within the luminous cloud, bringing the parts close together — and it has been said and noted that it sometimes occurs, but such a complete circle is extremely rare. The complete arc in this way will show a full circle. If a full circle is not seen — if it is asked: why is it that the rainbow and the clouds appear as they do —

It is a verified matter — this is an illusion, we say — this [argument] has no basis in the question, but the most correct [view] is that the matter is not [merely] an illusion, but rather [it is] real. The small mirror-like droplets [of water] reflect [light], and in the mirror an image is formed. It does not become complete [unless] like a mirror placed on one side; the two bows reflected from the sky appear to the eye as if in a mirror on the other side as well. If one looks at the water [reflected], one sees it inclined toward red — not [pure] blue — but rather dark blue. We say: likewise in a mirror, if the surface of the sea is greater and more expansive, the mirror-like [surface] shows [things]; for example, if a person looks at a red coral, the water appears inclined to red; if he looks at a blue coral, its image appears inclined to blue — as if its parts are inclined toward the blue color — and thus the light draws near to blue and the luminous [ray] is not transmitted [purely].

Since we have now explained this in detail, let us also describe the details of the rainbow (qaws quzaḥ), so that one who has studied the books of natural philosophy (ḥikma) may be rendered independent [of further sources]. The reason why [the rainbow] appears — that is, the cause of its formation — is that the small transparent water droplets [in the air] are arranged in a connected [manner], and like tiny mirrors...

When the sun is directly opposite — for example, the sun being on the eastern side and one being on the western side, or the sun being on the western side and one being on the eastern side — so that the rays are reflected from the watery particles, and those particles are gathered in a dense cloud in that place, and the rays penetrate through that dense cloud, and since in the mirror the darkness does not allow reflection, the rays of vision cannot perceive it and thus cannot convey an image; and the community of watery particles of the sky, when the sun is near the horizon, one sees the rainbow — because the reflection of the sun's heat increases, and since the subtlety of the watery particles is such that with that heat they are transformed in the air, and those watery particles must be situated in such a way that from the sun a straight line is drawn, and from the particles another line curves and goes around, and if it is equal to an arc, it would work — the angle of reflection from those watery particles must be equal to the angle of the ray along the straight line surrounding it, and those watery particles must be situated in such a way that the rays strike the watery particles; if that is so, then the observer will see the colors of the sun reflected from those particles as the shape of the sun's disk — as it has been stated — and from the particles one sees eight times as much as when near the sun, from the pale color and then from that to violet, in Turkish it is a compound of yellow and violet from that to a pistachio green, and from that to the one that is found as green, and in most cases three colors are seen. The variation of colors near the sun is considered to be a nightly matter, that is, near the sun—

From those parts [of water droplets], the rainbow displays the distances of those five colors, and likewise the manifold colors of the clouds and the watery particles within them are like a dense body whose colors are mixed and blended together.

In spring and autumn it appears over a mountain opposite, and if the arc of the rainbow rises higher, it would shrink entirely from above.

I will give a separate account so that the distinction becomes clear. As for the benefits of pure water:

It is an essential necessity; without it life cannot be found. If one asks why some people manage to live without it — despite its apparent necessity — we say: the purity of their constitution keeps them from needing it outright, being composed from the dryness of certain temperaments.

Among the benefits of pure water: it is found among us always, while impure water is sometimes found and sometimes not — even animal food and human nourishment may be unavailable. Yet pure water, if it reaches a human being, suffices him; indeed it is what makes a person truly human, as God Most High has said: 'And We made them among the angels.'

Among the benefits of pure water: it produces chyle from food, and after nourishment is obtained from it, it acts as a vehicle to carry the good substances in the food through the passages, causing them to flow through the conduits. It also keeps the body, clothing, and other things clean. Furthermore, it has this quality: it is more fluid than other liquids.

Among the benefits of pure water: if it is poured over a diseased limb that is inflamed — meaning while the swelling is present — it gives relief. And among its benefits: if one drinks pure water when it is lukewarm, it is a pleasant dissolvent.

Among the benefits of pure water: if pure water is mixed with something, it takes on its flavor and character — sometimes sweetness, sometimes sourness, sometimes saltiness, sometimes acidity — and it accepts the nature of whatever is mixed into it. Mixed with yellow it becomes yellow, mixed with red it becomes red, mixed with sweet it becomes sweet, mixed with bitter it becomes bitter. Thus the taste and quality of water is determined by what is blended into it.

As much as has been explained by way of example, since a little points to much — now, as for the benefits of salt water: One of them is this: that the sea, because its water is salty, does not stagnate. For if it were to remain stagnant for a time without being salty, its water would become putrid and malodorous, and the air in the surrounding regions would become corrupted; plagues would arise, and countless people would perish from it. Thus Divine Wisdom ordained that the sea's water be salty, so that this should not occur.

Another benefit is this: that in the great depths of the sea there are carcasses and corpses and decaying matter. Were the sea's water fresh and not salty, the power of decomposition in those carcasses would spread throughout the world, people would be harmed, and plagues would arise from the resulting putrefaction. But because the sea's water is salty, this does not come to pass, and those harmful things cannot cause corruption.

Another benefit is this: that because the sea's water is salty, pearls, ambergris, and other wonders that arise in the sea form therein — as will be described in detail in their appropriate sections.

Another benefit is this: that if the sea's water were fresh and not salty, the ships that sail upon it and mix their fresh water with it would find no buoyancy; they could not float and would sink. Because the sea's water is salty and dense, ships float upon it and people make their livelihood by traveling upon it.

Another benefit is this: that for difficult diseases, bathing in salt seawater brings healing and recovery, while drinking from springs in that region causes numerous ailments — as is recorded regarding mineral springs. But as for food and drink, the mineral spring water restores the hungry and brings health to the sick.

Another benefit is this: that the sea's water being salty...

For this reason, the seas near the shores are stirring and turbulent, and good salts are produced. God Most High has made the water of the sea extremely salty, so that vapors laden with impurities rise from it, and due to cold and moisture it rains upon the hills, and heavy rains descend so that blessings and abundance come forth. Among the wonders of divine creation, every food, drink, fruit, and need is found, so that what is needed by all who come to the shore — despite being in great need — is found in abundance, as in springs, drinking waters, lakes, pools, and wherever rain falls and floods come. As has been said, in Egypt, vapors suddenly rise, and among the wonders of craftsmanship, they are carried by the cold of the clouds, and their saltiness departs and they become pure water. And His Excellency — may God be glorified and exalted — has made the air like a wheel, turning the water of the seas and irrigating the gardens of the world, providing water of all kinds. The remainder collects in underground caverns and grottos, and serves the servants of God and animals. Among the wonders of God's craftsmanship, some waters flow into channels, some are overcome by air, and some — the salty water of the seas — overflow, so that humans and all other living creatures drown in them. Indeed, rather, there are many waters that are very beneficial. It is not surprising that some of them are beneficial in this world; however, since this world is the abode of impermanence and corruption, whatever has benefits also has harms. We shall also mention the harms of these waters, so that you may protect yourself from their injuries. But however harmful sweet water may be...

"Buri" (beaver/castor): It is such that its chest gland is well-known, and those who sit with it speak of it — "Buri" is such that drinking too much of its water weakens sexual desire and makes the constitution feeble. "Buri" is such that whenever one moves away from it and then returns after some time, drinking it again repeatedly on subsequent days — "Buri" is such that drinking hot water along with it is harmful as a firm remedy. "Buri" is such that drinking it harms the stomach and the brain. "Buri" is such that the one who drinks water pressed from it weakens the bowels and perception. "Buri" is such that every person who drinks it sinks and drowns in it — "Buri" is such that drinking too much of it brings on sleep, and the one fond of it ruins the land.

A story: In the year four hundred and fifty-something, a man from the region of al-Sham — a young man came, and a young lad from Ghulaj [a region] went to him and sat with him, and the people of that area told [the story] — none among the people who came there was harmed except the young man. In the end it came to this ruinous and widely harmful matter — and we seek refuge in God.

"Vebri" — It was such that there were many wounds upon the shore, and the water became salty and turbid. Verse: Keep your lips moist, / O physician, the eye and heart saw the water of the tress as water, "Vebri."
In that lake the water is very abundant; drink it and know that its water keeps the balance, and its riding is rough — but beware of its dusty turbidity.
There is also another benefit: "Meri" — it is a lake whose vapors are medicinal and purge the bile — "Vebri" — it is a lake [whose water]
makes thick humors thin — "Veri" — it is a lake that makes one who drinks of it laugh, rejuvenating old men — "Vebri" — it is a lake of la-samba [?]
whose [water] makes those who drink laugh repeatedly — "Vebri" — it is a lake whose foodstuffs, when altered, cause laughter and happiness — "Vebri" —
it is a lake that is extremely dangerous on the sea. Verse: Do not let it pass from your eyes — do not travel by sea,
for when you are like crystal, there is danger in it. SECOND CHAPTER: Concerning the accidents of the sea and what is upon the surface of the earth —
that is, the water surrounds all the earth, and the sea is situated in one place, and in one place its quantity is very great — entirely —
because God Almighty, among the wonders of His craft, [arranged] the shores such that if the water were not [held back by] the coasts,
naturally it would overflow and cover all the earth's surface, and its plains would be filled —
and then animals and plants would be annihilated. But His wisdom and judgment [ordained]
otherwise. It is known that the center of the sun differs from the center of the earth, so that as the sun revolves it comes close to one side of the earth
and moves away from the other side; as a result the water on [one] side becomes warm and its nature changes — and thereafter the second [consideration]:
The pole toward the north [is where] the sun [is] in the southern direction, and on the other side the sun is toward the north — the south
side is therefore greater [in heat], as is known, and the north is [cooler] — and thus the southern side [of the earth] ...

If one asks about the seas to the north, the northern side comes first. The seas on the southern side, compared to the gulf — that is, the mouth of the sea and its straits — if one asks about waters rising from the earth and flowing toward Damascus, and some say 'it came from that direction' and others contradict this, saying that the wind has spoken — the water flows in its natural course as the earth causes it to flow, and they see it thus. God Most High knows the truth of the matter. ——— And sometimes [the sea] rises, and the reason for this is that when the sun reaches [a certain position], the fine particles in the water become dissolved and dispersed, and they move through a vast expanse, pushing one against the other in the direction of Khurasan, repelling each other in five directions: east, west, north, south, and above. At one time, different flags appear on the shores of the sea, and the middle of the sea becomes [calm] while [the water] is [stirring]. The flood and waves of the sea do not cease, but they are not so great in the interior. And as for the properties of the tides — the ebb and flow caused by the moon — they had been mentioned and explained elsewhere in detail, though we did not mention them here completely, so that it may be known where the ebb and flow occur. The full details, to be known properly, [involve] causes that are hidden mysteries — namely that at the bottom of the sea there are hard rocks and stones, and when [the water] reaches them, it is reflected back, and the fine water of the sea [returns].

As long as it remains rarefied and subtle, it produces delicacy and refinement in the children it bears, and it inevitably increases in purity. When it becomes like pure water, it begins to collect in the depressions and lowlands, becoming cold, and the waters of the sea grow thick and cold, and the sea waters recede and diminish for fifteen days from the beginning of the month until its end, then return.

And the vital spirit of the sea — that is, the sea currents — is like the temperaments of a person; sometimes its motion is dominated by bile, sometimes by phlegm and black bile, in turns active then still. Its foods are sparse, its motion forceful, sometimes producing vigor and sometimes weakness.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, described the states of the sea in a subtle and eloquent phrase: 'The angel charged over the seas fashions a leg in the sea, and from that comes delight, then it withdraws and becomes a torrent.'

The scholars attributed this to the system of the tides, attributing it to natural causes, while the scholars of religious law attributed it to the angels charged over it.

Anecdote — [ascribed to] Muhammad ibn Zakariyya:

I asked Imam Abd al-Ghaffar al-Shami and said: I see the sea and its great wonders and currents. He said: It has two cycles each year — one in spring and one in autumn — and within those two seasons the bodily humors are set in motion, and in the other two seasons they move in equilibrium. Thus for six months the waters increase and for six months they decrease. Since you have heard the accounts of its states and its rulings and the rarities and wonders of the sea, let me now mention the wonders of the seas that surround the great world.

Third Chapter: On the Seven Seas.

In sum, among all the seas, the greatest is the Ocean (Bahr al-Muhit). Its name in Greek is 'Okeanos.' It is related from Ka'b al-Ahbar that God Almighty—exalted be He—created seven seas, and first He encompassed the Earth with the Ocean, so that the lands are surrounded within it like the white of an egg surrounds the yolk. And among these islands, some are inhabited—that is, with living creatures in them—and some are desolate. In detail, there are four thousand islands, of which twelve thousand are inhabited and twelve thousand are ruined, as they say. Three of these islands are known as the 'Khalidat' (the Eternal Islands / Canary Islands). On each one of them a column has been erected, on top of which a figure stands as tall as a man. On top of the column there is a figure in the form of a plumb-line, made of copper. And to its right and left there are other figures. These point with their hands, as if to say: beyond this point there is no passage—that is, no one passes beyond this boundary. It is said that the children of Athāmūth built these, and that Dhū al-Manār al-Akhīr built one of them. It is said that they were sun-worshippers. In this sea, coral trees grow; wherever one dives in it, one brings up red coral. It is related that this sea lies on the western lands, next to the city of Andalus (al-Andalus), on whose shore the Ocean lies, and no one who has ever embarked on a voyage into it has returned safely. As for the story of what happened in the time of Alexander Dhū al-Qarnayn, it is told that it became well known. This account is as much as the reliable sources record, and the story is this: that Alexander of the Ocean...

The true seas—whether one goes into them or not—the real seas that exist; as for the Ocean, let it be left alone.

As for the Narin Sea and the surrounding ocean, it is told that there came to its shores a captain, two meeting points from the west, who went to a special chief and mixed the hearts of men together. They sent out parties to the deep sea and beyond, and some said: 'We went to see what lay beyond the horizon, and no one had seen those fish before.' Many came and some said they went and returned, having found news and reported to the king of the land, saying: 'Do not waste time, for time is short and favors no one.' I traveled a certain distance and reached a place and met someone, and both parted ways. The people of the city dispersed, and a woman was given, and Alexander was informed, and they brought him gifts. He gave her to one of them, and from her children were born, and both the mother and daughter spoke, saying: 'Our king resembles a commander — they sent an expedition and traversed the sea, crossing eye to eye.' A man came and said: 'Let us make peace, because one ship crossed the living sea.' Then he said: 'In the end you have joined us — go and tell the king how it is.' The young man said: 'Our king surpasses Alexander, for his kingdom is greater than his kingdom, and his realm is even beyond that.' That is to say, the surrounding ocean of the west from the northern direction stretches and comes, and from there onward toward the heart — as for Jafar, he was taken by the people of Constantinople and they besieged it, and from there it goes onward until one reaches the Syrian Sea, which lies to the north, and rises to the land of Sicily parallel, and when one reaches the land of Bulgaria nearby, it is a great river at heart.

To the north of the Saqaliba (Slavs), at the first stage of the road toward the color known as Rang, in the direction of those who go toward the east, along that shore — there lie the lands of the Turks at their furthest extent. There are small mountains there and ruined settlements, one after another. That region and land is near Gog and Magog, to the east, and beyond it one arrives at the place called Salnaga (Selenga), which is also called Asmid. It is said to be in the direction of the Khatai (Cathay) sea, from the highlands of Khata and Hindustan. It is said that if one travels in two great directions, one of them toward the Kipchak steppe and the other toward the Jarim, then one arrives after that at a sea where trees grow one after another in succession, in the manner of the Jamal-Khata region. Going from there, one reaches the center of the world, for beneath it lies a great sea, encircling the region of Hindustan to its length, and the climes of India extend in length, and to the south the kingdoms stretch, and the mountains of Farkanel extend in their length, and beyond them are the kingdoms of Abyssinia and the lands of Andalusia, and the kingdoms extend westward to the shores. The sea encircles this world like a bowl, and Talmashdar and the surrounding sea — the islands (jazā'ir) therein are very numerous, as has already been mentioned, and their sizes are varied: some are a few farsakhs (leagues) and some are many farsakhs in extent, and one of the islands well known among them is the island of Wāq Wāq. And this Wāq Wāq — its trees are some two cubits tall, bearing fruit like shields, ornamented and colored and shaped, and as tall as a man. They have heads like human heads, hair like hair, eyes like eyes, ears like ears, and shapes like shapes. When the wind blows they call out 'Wāq Wāq.' It is said they resemble a person who speaks but does not speak. One speaks: • Then from that forest a voice arose • Toward the treetops it came along the branch •

...they came and the sounds echoed. The very first of the notable created things — by this sound, Eclipses (Ekliyos) come to observe.

The Encircling Ocean (Bahr al-Muhit): Among its well-known and inhabited islands are: the island of Ranj, the island of Saqaliyya (Sicily), the island of Qara, the island of Sas, the island of Rhodes, the island of Zanj, the island of Socotra, the island of Serendib (Sri Lanka/Ceylon), the island of Rijan, and the island of Ceylon (Sailan). From these detailed accounts it becomes clear that the Encircling Ocean — the Great Sea — surrounds all the regions of the world, and the gulfs and bays found throughout the world resemble one another, yet the Encircling Ocean remains separate from them. If anyone wishes, they can sail all around it without obstruction, as there is nothing to prevent them. The Caspian Sea (Jurjan Denizi) is also called Adayim Denizi; it is a remarkable sea.
