Rather, it is like the Encircling Ocean — what has been mentioned here is only a summary in proportion to what could be described. From now on, we will mention some of its wonders, as recorded in the books of the chronicles of the lands. Even upon it, devils, demons, and other spirits have settled and surround it. At its base are other sources of corruption, and within it is a prison on an island where an angel dwells in opposition. There too are mountains, and the shrine of Hazrat Sulayman (Solomon), peace be upon him, where Mika'il (Michael) resides, and a noble body is present there. On that island is a wondrous palace, and within the island there are creatures; and there are also great castles and fortresses. In it there are fish of wondrous and varied forms, and along the shores of the ocean there are towns and cities. Sometimes creatures appear and disappear — sometimes they appear as crystal, sometimes as flames, sometimes as mountains of strange and wondrous shapes; sometimes people see themselves in them, and some find themselves reflected. The creatures of the ocean — the seas in the midst of which is life and death — these are great seas. Connected to the Encircling Ocean from the eastern side is the Red Sea (Bahr al-Qulzum), and beyond the Encircling Ocean to the south is the greatest sea. There is also a sea called Bahr al-Hind (Indian Ocean), which is of great waves and immense shores, with powerful currents; within it the ebb and flow of the sea occurs, and it is connected to the Persian Sea. In it there are whirlpools, and it has been said that those who fall into them — their description has been given — fish come out from the water as large as a fortress. One should go and see this for themselves, and upon an island there are iron cliffs and barren grounds. Among its settled inhabitants there is a type of white bird, different from owls, and among them...

And these sailors traveled by sea, passing through the region of the Green Sea (Bahr al-Akhdar) along the coasts of Fars, reaching Basra, along the sea of Sindh on its western side, passing through the provinces of Makran, Kirman, and Fars and onward to Abadan, heading southward toward Bahrain and the Yemen coast, and Oman and the land of Najd. Passing along the coasts for two or three hundred farsakhs, one comes to two mountains there which are extremely arid and desolate, and the region is very difficult to pass through safely. The water of this sea rises from its depths and its water is different from other seas in quality. We have already mentioned some of its wonders previously; now let us describe what came to mind. In Balkar — which is said to have many wonders — among them is that white horses are bred there, trained and paired together, and the region's horses are famous for their qualities and are held in esteem. Among the fine horses there are some of the color of sugar, though they are not considered of great value. There is also a great island there called Rāybaj, within which are trees like gold trees in their appearance, tall and broad, abundant in their yield. And in that land there grows musk, such that whoever passes through it is perfumed with the scent of musk.

On this island there are animals whose musk glands produce genuine musk.
There are white monkeys there, small like sparrows in size and strength, and some monkeys are
blue-white and black, and their bodies are not very large — they live among one another.

On it there are parrots: white, grey, red, yellow, and black — they imitate whatever sounds they hear.

On it there are also human-like creatures, grey and white-and-black in body, and they have no speech.
They fly about; they are wild by nature, and when approached they cry out, and their words are entirely unintelligible.

There are trees there, and cranes come and go, flying from tree to tree and perching.

There is a type of creature there that resembles a cat in shape, having wings from its neck all the way to its rump, and its wings are of no use whatsoever and provide no benefit.

There are mountain foxes there, resembling domestic donkeys in appearance, their backs spotted, their tails like a horse's tail, and their braying like that of a she-camel.

On the island called Rāmnī there are places of fine quality, and the goods and provisions there are abundant, and the cities are numerous. Their height is four spans [arm-lengths], their hair is red, they climb extremely high into the trees, and no pleasant creature goes near them.

On this island camphor trees, jiran trees, and baqam [brazilwood] trees grow. It is said that there is a light found in the thorns of certain plants there, and there are elephants which lift great loads with their trunks.

Waqwaq

In that direction there are trees bearing all kinds of fruit, and there are also poplar and plane trees. Indeed, the sounds of voices are heard there, and the people of that land come to listen and to interpret them. Near the island called Jazīrat al-Banā there lives a people who go naked, with white and beautiful complexions. People who come from afar say that there are large areas of flat land there, with people who have long hair and long limbs — and among them too there are human-like beings. Near that island there is also an island called Ṭūrān, with a kind of flat, pleasant terrain. A type of creature resembling a monkey lives there, and camphor is also found there. It is reported that when Alexander came to this island, he found a people whose bodies were like human bodies, but whose heads were shaped like those of woodpeckers — some male and some female. In their outward form one could take them for humans, and indeed from a distance they appeared human, but up close one could tell they were not quite human.

And when the waves of that sea increase and the dark clouds gather, the birds land on four fathoms [of water]. In the region of Qarajah-Ada (a small island near Malta), there are birds that never look toward the direction of a human eye. It is said that they do not land [on the water], and at a known time the musk-deer comes down to the water of Sirsil to drink. The creature called 'Amuba resembles [something], it is a creature from whose body, when struck at the joint, blood flows — it comes from [that] region. In the western province, the Maltabak is clearly visible. And on certain islands of that sea there is a species of animal with multiple heads and faces, large curved teeth, and two wings. The dark-colored ones among them, when they fly, their places of landing are known.

[Marginalia, right column:] Noted: the tongue of the infidels is depicted here.
[Marginalia, lower right:] My dear, the two of them are depicted here.

The turtle lives in water and is among the animals that walk on dry land; it is said to be one of the most cautious creatures. It retreats into its shell when frightened, and draws in its head, legs and tail, becoming like a stone. It is observed that its gait is slow and it has a hard shell.

[Illustration label:] Image of the turtle

[Illustration label:] Image of the Khidr fish (sturgeon)

In the sea there is also a fish called the 'Silan.' It is said that when two of these come together, they circle about rapidly, then they crash into one another and scatter apart. This is a type of creature found in the depths; it has layers of scales, one layer upon another, and two fins, and it is counted among the large fish.

In the sea there are also certain rocks and reefs where living creatures cling; when they are removed from those rocks they perish. They are exceedingly hard, and are used by craftsmen as a kind of abrasive. In the sea there are also others of their kind.

An account of how an enemy — one who stored away provisions for himself — settled near a watering place, and how the merchants came to him.

A Story: A certain merchant told [this tale]:
Among our traveling companions there was a blind man who had arrived at a waystation. A firm rope was lowered down [into a well] with enough length to reach the bottom. Now, although he was blind, he had heard about a place of extraordinary provisions and commerce. So he set out, and when he had descended a good distance, he said: "I can no longer hear anything." He kept going down along the rope until he reached the bottom of the well, where he found himself in the darkness.

He called out: "What do you see around you?" They told him they could see black birds flying over the surface of the sea. The blind man began to weep and said: "I can see nothing — why should I have come down at all?"

Shortly after, he passed by, and our group fell into that whirlpool. Those black birds, as it turned out, were angels — whenever anyone fell in, the people inside would perish. The whole company was confounded, astonished, and helpless. Then the blind man said with half-cleverness: "I will find for you a way of salvation — I will deliver you without sugar [i.e., freely]."

The company agreed. He reached in among those who were there — the sailors and crew — and they were brought to him. He bound them with ropes to the rafts. Then he gave the order and they were told to tie the ropes of those people together and cast them into the sea.

They did so. Then the blind man told the boatmen to take a plank and a board and paddle [away]. They began to row and pushed away from that whirlpool. Afterward, the blind man had the ropes cut, reached safety, and thus they were saved.

The Sea of India (Bahr al-Hind): This is a great sea, full of benefits beyond count and great dangers within it. It connects to the encompassing ocean (al-Bahr al-Muhit) and borders the land of Sind. Kalkuland and Katabad lie written along its shores. In former times its waters were said to be conveyed to the region known as the Land of Kahk, whose king built fortresses along its coasts, and it was full and overflowing without end.

Some have related that this sea was conquered by a certain power, and it became like a place of divine mercy, surpassing description. When the sun enters Virgo (Sunbula) the sea approaches the region and the darkness of the Indian Ocean increases tremendously and its waves swell.

When the sea's motion becomes quite violent and its currents extremely difficult, then when the sun passes through that constellation and moves away, the darkness lifts and the sea grows calmer, making navigation possible.

When the sun enters Sagittarius (Qaws) and moves to that region, the sea reaches its extreme state, for then the great ships and vessels find their way with difficulty.

Now since I have mentioned some of the conditions of the Indian Ocean and recorded what was to be recorded, I shall henceforth recount its wonders and marvels.

Now, as for Balkakir: it is said that certain of the inhabitants there are much taller than others — taller by many handspans.

The Island of Burtayil Sar: It lies near the enclosed sea, and is extremely close. In it there is a great abundance, and there dwells in it a people whose skins have shed their color and who are bare-backed. Their livestock — horses and sheep — are exceedingly numerous there.

These people's clothing is light. They come to the market bringing nutmeg and saffron and cloves and
noble [goods]. They arrive at the port, and there are many in Istanbul who come and buy cloves and nutmeg.
Their natural disposition is such that they go to the market and bring things together. They stand on the shores of the sea
and settle at a place and go in the morning. The merchant gathers a certain amount of cloves
and goes to market, finding more cloves each time.
They go and gather the cloves and if they are satisfied with the price of the cloves, they are pleased. The clove merchants
take the cloves and go to the market at dawn, selling both cloves and other goods.
They go under water and dive and return as if searching for fresh cloves to gather.
The wise elder said: a group of people went around the island and saw
their faces resembling Turks, their chests broad, their ears large, and their women adorned. When first
I saw them, my eyes were filled with tears, suddenly they disappeared. They said the clove market is done.
Thus it became known to me that no one desires to be seen by those people.
Then it was related about this place—on the island of clove markets:
They traded there. It is also narrated that on this island, when passing by the shore, stones
came flying, white stones falling, and on this island there are mountains and in them strange things.
Sounds of trumpets, drums, and pipes are heard, and sometimes voices of singing are heard.
The people of the sea who come to this port say: I saw strange things there that I cannot describe. God alone knows all.

And in that region there are people whose bodies are like human bodies, but their heads are like the heads of dogs.

And on this island there are people who have no heads, and their eyes are in their chests.

[Marginal note in red:] Figure of a headless person

And from that island onward is [a place called] Balamit, which is a fertile land where sandalwood, Indian spikenard, camphor and various wonders are found. The inhabitants are cunning deceivers; they lure the unwary, and when travelers pass through, the people of that region seize them and carry them off — and in that region [the account continues]...

There is a place called Yaqub Qarshi, along its shore. If the desert waters are dry by day, white stones appear; if not, black stones appear. From there one ascends and a falcon-like tower launches into the air, and by climbing one reaches a great island called Qadd, and there are palaces of crystal and clear rock-crystal there, finer than anything seen, as a guide to its safety. In that exalted palace, soldiers come as visitors from the direction of Marv, and one of the king's soldiers goes among the nightingales but cannot proceed; he approaches that great palace and enters its vast interior, sending forth the trust of Noah, so that the angels carry it away—five or so of them—thus Alexander had those waters brought, and Ptolemy recorded it. The inhabitants are like men hewn from rock, their hair like streams, their dogs like sheep in appearance, their bodies lean and spare. When Alexander's army came out, they hurled stones at them, and when Alexander's army arrived there, the philosophers informed him of it, and they came and saw, and everyone who enters that palace becomes unable to leave it and falls unconscious, and the angels carry them away; none who entered it ever returned. And in its crenellations there are lamps glowing like light by day and by night, and no one can look at them. There is a nearby island called Jaba, where there is a great mountain, atop which is a treasure, and one can see it by day, but none can reach it, and on that same island there are in abundance: aloe wood, bananas, bitter orange, ginger, and sugar cane, and the soil there is exceedingly fertile. And on that island there is a wondrous fish; from beneath its chin flows a moisture, and with that moisture one may write on paper—what is written cannot be seen by day, but when night comes it becomes visible.

Whoever reads these luminous lines and comes to know them should write it as a prescription, and there is a people there in the form of humans whose mothers' faces are on their chests.

[miniature: a bald, stocky figure standing on an island with a tree]

And on this side of the island there are creatures whose appearance is like that of humans, with crowns of gold upon their heads, wearing garments, nursing at the breast, and there are stone-like forms among them. The name of their transformation is Badr, and the foremost of the noble islands lies opposite. There stand the animals, the rivers, the dancers, those who worship them, and the islands of the Indian Ocean among the three islands. These lie close together on the shore, connected, with thunder and lightning following one after another, with winds, birds, and other creatures passing continuously, among them those birds that do not land. And in the region of the island of Sidon there is a lake whose circumference takes about a month to traverse. In it are wondrous trees, strange and ancient, and in the vicinity of Sidon a king once spread his domain, and the people of that land built upon a throne of gold, constructing upon the rocks a great edifice.

Among the wonders: The decorated throne, and how Solomon sent his army, subduing the kingdoms, and after that the king sat upon the throne and sat upon it, and the minister arose and sat.

Among the islands of the Indian Ocean is the island of Qas. The word 'Qas' in truth [refers to] a creature that lives in the shallows, four-legged, resembling a tortoise in its shell and eyes and mouth. It has a voice that is continuous and very prolonged; it cries out with a sound like that of a man reduced to misery. For six months it appears in the shallows, and for six months it goes somewhere unseen and eats nothing.

Among the islands of the Indian Ocean is the island of Qamar. All the trees of these shallows [produce] sandalwood and aloe-wood. Its aloe-wood is of the finest quality and is known by another name; it is among the famous [products] of the islands of the Indian Ocean.

Among the islands of the Indian Ocean is the island of Sayf. It is a very fine shallow place. Its water is abundant, and there are many kinds of trees: foodstuffs and taro, camphor, rice, banana, coconut, sugarcane, sandalwood, aloe (laqm), and aloe-vera (ṣabrān) trees grow there. Aloe-wood also grows there — it is called pressed/distilled aloe-wood — and in these shallows...

Among the creatures [of the sea]: the forbidden and unlawful fish are known, and the creatures thereof — among them is a fish that is green in color, with a head like that of a snake; whoever encounters it, it spreads harm upon him.

And there is a fish in the warm waters, and within it there is something like oud (agarwood), and it is deadly. And what is called Tawka-kaw — no creature encounters it except that it kills it outright.

[Marginal note in red:] Depiction of the Kaw-lah

And there is a creature therein that has two forms: one of its aspects is in the form of a human — whoever draws near to it [is in danger].

The dog-like creature: it resembles a dog in its body, but its tail is like that of a fox.

[upper illustration: a two-headed being]

There is an animal in the land of Zanj (East Africa) that resembles a poor man in shape; when looked at, it has a neck with horns. It is called Mijraj. Its special property is that all beasts of prey flee from it.

[lower illustration: a fox-like creature with horns/antlers]

There is another creature such that if its skin is scraped and rubbed on the teeth, it whitens them and strengthens the gums; and if a piece of it like a shell or a chip the size of a nail is placed in a pot, it will bind together all the people of that region.

[Right margin, red:] This is the image of the two-headed man.

[Lower margin, red:] Image of the Mijraj.

Among the islands of India is the island of Serendib [Sri Lanka], one of the islands of India. In this place there is a mountain, and it is said that Adam descended there. When one approaches it, they say that Adam came first and they visit it in his name. They say that among the teeth of Adam, peace be upon him, a sea creature came out and became a great king, and from its grace came varieties of rubies. On that mountain are beautiful colored stones and fragrant trees, and arrows grow there as well. It is always green there. And if one sails by it for a distance of about a mile in each direction of the sea, pearls wash in, and they are found in the surrounding waters among the islands of India. Among the islands is the island of Shankuna [Seychelles/a named island]. There they speak of certain serpents, and a woman whom they call the Serpent's Lady. A church, a fortress, a pavilion, a dome, and four arches have been built there, and it is said that whoever settles there is drowned.

And from the Sea of India, in the island of Ward (Rose Island), there are red roses, and they are brought back and exported. There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God. And in that sea there are various islands, and some animals are found there, but they are of little benefit. The Kalima of Shahada has not been accepted there. The Persian Sea — it is said that its gold is preserved. Certain rivers flow there from the mainland, and those rivers are blessed, and there are fig trees along them which provide remedies. It is less turbulent and agitated than other seas. The ocean sea has its tides and ebbs, and it was mentioned earlier that the Sea of India and the Persian Sea — their tides were explained when they were described. If the direction of the Persian Sea is connected to the Sea of India, their channels are different, for the waves of the Persian Sea run deep, while the Sea of India is calm. When the Persian Sea is calm, the waves of the Sea of India run deep. When the sun enters Pisces and approaches Scorpio in autumn, then when the sun continuously enters Pisces, the difficulties are described. When the sun enters Sagittarius toward the end of autumn and approaches the quarter, it returns. Its benefit is that in the spring, toward the end of spring, when the sun enters Gemini, various Chinese goods become available. The merchants of the Persian Sea benefit greatly, and near its coasts and shores pearls and coral are found, and rubies, gold, iron, copper, prayer mats, carnelians and various things, and ambergris are obtained. Many of its islands are renowned in the Sea of China. Bangalus — some call it Kanjalu — it is said there are few people there, but they are described as passing through.

Among the wonders that were brought from Alexander's treasury as a gift, and whose image was drawn and recorded, is a bird known in the arts [of natural history] as the first of birds.

Its nature and characteristic is this: it honors and shows kindness to its parents. When one of a pair [of its kind] grows old and can no longer fly, two of its companions take it under their wings, carry it, bring it to a place of shelter, and tend to it as one would a sick person — some say two companions carry it from the open country to the meadow, and from there to the waterside and to fruit-bearing trees, bringing it food from tree to tree until it recovers, not leaving it without water and nourishment. They say it thus honors and shows kindness to its parents, repaying what was done for it in youth.

Another marvel: it knows — it is said — the exact moment when a storm will come: fourteen days before, it settles and remains calm. During those fourteen days the sea stays still, the waves subside, and sailors can cross safely. They call this bird [the halcyon]; it is said to nest on the surface of the water, and when it settles the sea becomes safe for those who sail it.

The whale [balıq]: sometimes it passes by one another, and sometimes it appears at the surface of the sea, and it is seen again at the depths of the sea.

[Marginal note]: A note on the illustration of the whale [balıq].

Two kinds of pearls: those that form around a nucleus in the sea and those that are found loose — these are the ones into which drops and moisture enter. They are found at the bottom of the sea, in the northern winds and the summer heat. Sometimes they grow at sunrise and sometimes they grow without ever becoming full. At midday the heat of the sun is intense and causes the liver to move vigorously, so that the pearl may be spoiled. The oyster shell opens its mouth toward the sky when the north wind blows and the heat of the sun is strong, so that the wind and warmth of the sun enter it. Thus the pearl is formed inside it — as Mawlana (Rumi), God have mercy on him, says in the Masnavi: 'O spring, the thirsty eye is not filled / the oyster that is not content with the surface does not find the pearl.' If the oyster is full of water containing foreign matter, the pearl that forms in it will be yellow in color, tending toward that hue. When the oyster is on a reef and the people of the season know it, from that early time the pearl is unripe; but eventually at the end of its time it surfaces and the pearl becomes pure and clear. If the oyster is turned upside down, the pearl changes shape and becomes different.

As for the special properties of the oyster shell: it is truly beneficial, for if it is burned and reduced to powder and then mixed with honey and applied to the eye, it benefits eye pain. It removes the opacity of the eye, bestows clarity and sweetness, and strengthens it. If one of the pearls found inside the oyster is placed upon its walnut and positioned there, it repels harm and injury.

In its middle there is a hump; from the side its bite cuts through and if it encounters a sea creature it tears it into two pieces. Its mouth is at the front and its tail is at the back, and it has a slit [opening].

Travelers and sailors relate that in the region of Mulk-Walāya there are wonders [to be seen].

Concerning the wonders of the island: its marvels are many, and among the wonders of divine creation and the marvels of God's creatures — a man from Isfahan turned back and related that he had become destitute and loaded his pack, then by chance mounted a horse and set out toward the Persian Sea. Along the way there were many merchants, and they said to him: 'Is there any remedy to be free of this poverty?' He replied: 'If you will ransom one soul among the Turks, I will do it.' He went and informed the household of Asaf who were there, giving news to his family, saying: 'Ransom six of our souls among the Turks.' The next day he said: 'Among those belonging to Asaf's household there were many merchants; he gave a firm account.' They quickly fulfilled their obligations to his family and gave them full care as promised. He said: 'What good will come of it?' He said: 'The chief goes face to face toward the island, and there he beats the drum continuously, so that the people come face to face. That great bird was there; the chief took the answer.' He drove away those who had perished, and the ones who remained were wandering. He beat the drum and spent the night; every time he came he beat it, then it came down, swooped, and chased away the chief, who fled and ran, disappearing from sight. He then walked on. After that, he wandered that island. Suddenly he saw a great hollow tree, and creatures without number — out of fear of that hollow tree he called out; he was frightened and cried out, and a woman beside him calmed and reassured him. A great bird came and perched on that hollow tree; out of fear he let go and walked for many hours. In the morning, that woman flew away and he walked alone that day along that road, and he found his life preserved, as it has been told.

I was overcome with shame and grief. I went to the falcon-keeper's lodge and arrived there, and he lodged me. In the morning he opened [the cage] and the bird flew away and departed, and in the evening it returned by itself, without any fuss, and entered its lodging. I entered, and I became familiar and comfortable with the bird-keeper. One morning when it was light, I set out from the lodge, and there I saw the master of the place — may God spare the lodge's falconer — he told me: 'I will take you safely to the place you wish, for the falconer's sake.' I climbed into the air and looked down; my heart sank, and truly I was confounded. Again I considered releasing the falcon, but I bore patience and endurance. I endured much hardship and difficulty, and I said to the falcon: 'Save me and release me from this,' yet no one heard me from afar. Thereafter we passed over a sea and arrived at a cape — after every cape yet another appeared — and the masters carried us on, one after another until finally they left me on a shore in that condition, and all of them gathered around me. They took me to their place and spoke to me in their language — a man who knew it — and I ended up describing my whole situation. A story worth marveling at: they brought food, and I ate, and for several days they showed me honor and generosity. After several days I went out for a walk and I saw a great ship anchored nearby. A merchant who was trustworthy and sincere came forward, recognized me, hurried toward me and embraced me, and said he would help me reach my destination and would arrange matters. A story worth marveling at: they bade me farewell with thanks and prayers and blessings.

The Sea of Qulzum (Red Sea): There is no way to cross it by boat unless one has a skilled navigator. To its south lie certain lands, and to its western side lie the western lands, while to its eastern side lie the eastern lands. It is situated there. The city of Qulzum — after which the sea is named — stands on its shore, and within it and around it are well-known cities and prosperous lands. There Pharaoh and his army were drowned, and it is a place of awesome, terrifying passage.

And it is said that he traveled through the lands and could not find a kingdom. He came to a mountain and went to Abyssinia; its king cut off one of his mounts and sent it away. Thus he submerged the first kingdom and came to its border, reaching as far as Persia and elsewhere. He traveled through those lands and their magnetic mountains drew the nails from ships, causing them to sink. From there he went and in that place a white cotton-like substance appeared at festival time. If they came to that kingdom and passed through, they would catch from the sea whatever they wanted, and no one would die there, as we shall explain from what is known. In the chapter on the island of Taran, which is close by: this island is six miles long and on it lives a people called the Banu Akhdan. Their food is fish only, for nothing grows there and no animals are found. Their drinking water is not sweet. Their houses are made of the wood of broken ships and planks. The water of the sea comes to their people, and near there is a mountain which is called Util, firmly set. Two or three men could barely carry what comes from it. It is in those lands where the event occurred when Pharaoh and his army were drowned, and the news reached the region known as Jazmah. The Samaritans: there is a people there called the Samaritans who worship a calf. The story of al-Jassasah: and nearby is an island called al-Jassasah, and on it is a creature that gathers news and reports it to the Dajjal. The companions, having shown mercy, the preacher stood up and gave a sermon of admonition, saying: let there be unity, let there be one community. I gathered them together, and informed them that news had come that those from your people who returned had been detained. They were firmly taken to an island where they had seen an animal. They said to him: we have not seen its like. He said: I am going to investigate it. He said: one of them told me that news had spread that it had grown enormous, settling in a place where the person there longs for you. Come inside and eat, and go show it without concealing anything. They asked those present from which community and which land they came, and they answered. After that, in a similar way, they counted the men of Zarʿ and the men of ʿAnan. They also asked the cavalry about it, and answered and said that among them was one who could settle the matter. Among those who settled it: I rescued forty of the captives and traveled through the inhabited lands, wandering across the face of the world, and I intend to visit Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem — may God ennoble them — and to know all of them. Among the other animals found there and around it are certain animals and others. I left the companions and the people behind, and I set out alone. From that sea I reached an island called Dunuza (or Fanuda), near a region called Bulata, where there is a city. From its white stone, so many people come — in its markets, in its caravanserais, in its homes — there is such noise and bustle as you have never heard. And at night the merchants spread out, and its city is so astonishing that whoever arrives there lodges in Bulata. Its waters flow pure, coming from springs within, bearing the fragrance of camphor. Near Bulata there is a great mountain. They say that around it, there is a cloth woven like embroidered brocade; whoever spreads it out and a sick person lies upon it, they recover their health. And they say this cloth is found in a certain treasury, and becomes more abundant.

And beyond that sea there is an island called 'Awr (the Bald), and it is a great settlement whose trees shed their bark entirely.

Anecdote: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Tarraj said in his book of reports: I was told, and I witnessed it myself — a man came from the districts to this island, and I sailed there and found a people...

The nightingales were mostly gathered together, a group of them had brought word to the kings and rulers. The kings had them placed in a cage for that purpose. One day I climbed up onto a terrace and asked someone passing by, 'Where have you come from?' I said, 'I have come from here.' They said, 'We found no one to tell us.' I ate some of what was found along the road. Suddenly one day a group appeared in the middle, among them. I asked, 'I hear there are enemies nearby who attack this region; the women came just now and most of us were left without eyes to see.' Suddenly I saw many beautiful birds landing in that area, gathered in a flock, occupied among the people. One of them came and picked up a stick and began to kill the birds one by one, until it was done. The people were displeased, saying: 'If you find someone like this, it might be that we will not see them again.' I went back and shot arrows, on another day someone came straight [toward us].

And this is also evidence of its [the tortoise's] nature: that one day the physician Aristotle came...

Among the wonders of Khurasan: there is a region where a people live who have been brought together; their bodies are small and short in stature, and they come from beyond a certain island. Among those peoples there are some who resemble humans in body but whose faces are like those of dogs; they are said to eat meat raw.

And in a certain marsh there is a people who say: 'There is no one more capable than us.' These are their ways.

A Story: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Turraji al-Dimashqi said:
While traveling the world, I came across a man in Rum (Anatolia/Byzantine lands) who had very long nails. I asked him what he was and where he came from. He disagreed with me and, taking me out from that place, brought me to an island. There I saw a people whose faces were like the faces of dogs and whose bodies were like human bodies. One of them came toward us with a staff and struck, driving us back. Then a man came — the chief of those people and of their other body parts as well — and we understood that these were indeed human children, and there was a sick man there...

They did many things and sent away those fine people. He said to them: 'Without you this land— go and tell Samarra, for I have heard this news, and certainly from here I know nothing of Samarrand. And this sick person remained— the sick man said: They told me there is no one in Lochkun, I cannot go out into the open fields at all, so let it be known that these young men came and circled around and the smell of a person lingered there. And they came and said to those: Go under such-and-such a tree and you will be saved. All of them I ran, going nowhere, finding nothing, they came to their houses and could not find me, and fell and stumbled and called out: Go under that tree! And they went. At that time they turned back and left, and from there I descended, I saw people under the trees going away. I saw them from afar and their forms were beautiful. One of them suddenly came running and took my hand, and said nothing. Before I could say anything, suddenly one of them came running, took my hand and put it on its neck and mounted me, and before I could resist it carried me swiftly. I wanted to stop but it would not let me control the reins. My strength was overcome and I was defeated, it carried my mount and overcame it, as I went under those trees I had been for a short while going around, and suddenly my eyes fell and I saw by those trees— my grapevine staff, which I recognized as the one that had grown from a cutting of my grapevine, and immediately I dropped the reins—

The first [wonder]: There is a fish called Gokcheburge [or similar], which, when it comes near any drum sound, it rushes to catch it and tears it apart.
The second: When this fish wants to approach it [prey], those who drum it chase and catch it.

[Marginal note in red:] This is the image of the sawfish (minshar).

There is a light, swift fish in the sea called Bal [swordfish/sawfish]. When it hunts, it causes great distress and lamenting among [the other fish].
When it shows no mercy and comes with its two fins, every time a fish passes by swiftly,
it cuts it out of the water with force and strikes it, causing it to settle there and be consumed.
It strikes with its fins like a sword, cutting each fin, drowning them, drumming and striking,
chasing and catching them. And when the Baluq [fish] sees — that is, when it waves its fins and opens its mouth —
it turns toward it for a long time, submitting as God the Most High has created a fish
that has no equal; it remains alone, and it is called by this name [the sawfish/minshar].

The first sea is called the Bahr al-Falak (Sea of the Celestial Sphere); its fish are like those that swim in its depths, going down and coming up, and the angels watch over them. It is said that in its waters amber is found, as large as a camel, and the people of the coast come to it and gather it. The scent of ambergris is there, though not considered as valuable as that of the Sea of the Maghrib.

The Sea of the Maghrib is also called the Sea of Syria and the Sea of Constantinople, because it borders those regions and the Strait of Constantinople. It begins from the Ocean on the eastern side from Andalusia, passing to the north through the land of the Franks (France), then westward through the lands of Rum (Byzantium/Anatolia), reaching the Strait of Constantinople, then turning southward along the coasts toward Tripoli, the coasts of Syria and Antioch, where one finds large islands: the islands of Andalusia (Iberian coast), Majorca, Sicily, Africa (Ifriqiya), Cyprus, and Rhodes, and others similar.

In sum, this sea was created by God Almighty — glory and majesty be to Him — for the benefit of all creation, so that people might live and profit by it. Some have reported that this sea was separated from the great Ocean, and it has been related in the accounts of Egypt that this sea came from the direction of the Ocean. When Pharaoh and his army were destroyed and drowned in it, a certain king came and conquered Egypt with his forces, and since he was weakened, the king of Rum (Byzantium) coveted Egypt. The king of Egypt then, on the advice of his wise men, opened a channel from the Western Ocean toward the Maghrib side, through the cities and villages of Qaydoobaja (Cadiz?) and its surrounding towns.

The sea of Egypt on one side and Rome on the other, coming together between them, so that on one side are Muslims and on the other Christians. This is called the Junction of the Two Seas (Majma' al-Bahrayn), where the Sea of Rome meets the Sea of the West (Mediterranean). The width of this strait is three leagues and its length is several parasangs. At that strait there is ebb and flow of the tide: once because of the constellation of the Crab and once because of the constellation of the Scorpion — for when the sun rises, the Sea of the West churns and overflows toward the Levantine Sea; and when the sun reaches its zenith, the Levantine Sea overflows toward the West; and when the sun sets, the Western Sea again churns and overflows toward the Levant; and when it reverses, the opposite occurs. Among the islands to be described there, one island is called the Island of the Junction of the Two Seas. On it there is a great building like a lighthouse, made of squared stones fitted together without mortar, with no door, hollow inside, more than one hundred cubits tall. At its summit a rope is fastened, by which a man climbs up. It is said this is most likely a signal-tower: there is no passage here, and it was built to repel enemies and to block them. So it has been shut off and made into a sea-fortress. It is necessary for a ruler to devise strong measures to protect his subjects and repel enemies, and to undertake difficult deeds — and to build lighthouses tall and strong, made of foreign stone and fitted rock so that no one can scale or grip it from the outside, and made solid and without a door so that no one can penetrate it from within, and most likely fixed with ropes like...

In the sea of Darkness [the Atlantic/Black Sea], the king fashioned an image in Kondovunk [a place name], the like of which in permanence has no equal — it is established as a throne. And they say this is a talisman: whoever cuts off this strait will no longer be able to come from the Sea of Darkness to cause harm [to this land]. Thus this construction preserves the welfare of the subjects [ra'aya] until the Day of Resurrection.

And there is an island called Tenes in the Mediterranean Sea, near the city of Bolatiq, and around it there are many towns and villages. On that island, from a certain place in the sea, fish come in the beginning of the season; first one kind of fish comes, then after it another kind comes, then sugar is obtained from it. One kind is a white fish, and the harvest of pressing and grinding yields an abundance, and among the fish there are various kinds of mullet, and a certain fish there called Baluad, and some say that the birds that descend upon it number eighty-eight species of fish. It is found among the islands, and its special quality is that in it there are harmful living creatures like scorpions. And there are many people there, both scholars and righteous men, and in it are found precious garments and fine peacocks.

And another island is Sicily, in which there is a great city, and in it are found many towns and all kinds of creatures, humans and others, and many cattle and flocks, and there is a great mountain there called Etna, where the ancients used to go up to see it; fire comes out and smoke rises from it, and near that island, from a distance of twelve miles, if one approaches like a serpent's tongue, the wind carries it and it falls down, and when it descends it becomes like thin flat stones, and they sell it throughout the kingdom. And another island called Naum is in the sea, and on its trees the fruits and blossoms are so numerous that people fill sacks full from them and take them away.

And another island is Crete; Abu Hamid has said: on that island there is a mountain, and on that mountain there is a church, and that church is ruined, and on top of that church there is a dome, and on top of that dome...

There is a crow there: in that village there is a window, and opposite that church there is a mosque. People come to visit it, and prayers offered at that mosque are answered. It is incumbent upon the people of that church, whenever a Muslim comes, to receive them as guests. The crow perches on the window of that church and thrusts its head inside and calls out — it calls out as if to say: 'A guest has come!' — and whenever the guest arrives, it calls out so that the people of the church may know and prepare food and provisions accordingly. The people of the church: that crow is always there; whenever it comes to eat, [they ask] where it has come from and where it is going.

Image of a Mosque and a Church

And there is an island called Talat, as Abu Hamid has mentioned: on this island sheep roam freely and they grow exceedingly fat. From the arrival of summer onward, because of their great abundance, they flee from human beings. Those who come there are the local people who take sheep from the herdsmen, taking three at a time. The sheep on that island are so numerous that even if all the ships came to the port and loaded their full cargo of sheep, the number of sheep would not diminish, and on that island nothing other than sheep is found.

Fourth Chapter: On sea creatures — in this chapter we will describe the creatures that are found [in the sea]. Among those creatures that have been mentioned by chance, one [account comes from] a man of the Maghreb, Ibn Marwani, who after a long journey arrived by the sea of the Berbers, and our elders have recorded that a Slavic slave came with him, intending to fish that night — this has been mentioned and he was left there. He was caught, and it was a span in length, and the craftsman [had made it so that] behind its ear there was [something like] a lala...

And Buri [a type of fish]: Abu Hamid of Damascus recounts that he was traveling on the Mediterranean Sea, and a great wave opened up. I first saw among them oranges, as if freshly fallen from a tree — I thought to myself and picked one up. I looked around the shore in the shallows at the edge of the water, and saw a young creature growing up there in the water, and I was capable [of approaching] it, and I wished to cut it with a blade, but I saw it had no head, no eyes — nothing but a mouth pressing against the stone from below, and its flesh was there inside it. It drew me in with its force, [and I pulled myself] away from its mouth; the water coming from it was cold, running out like something poured, red and fine. I regretted [approaching] it; it moved its mouth and breathed — and this was Buri. It is found on the western sea. A bird comes there, as the overseers say, which brings blessed [things]; it brings [them] to a fearful place nearby, or to an island where animals live, and it calls out gently and sets up its station. When the station descends it gives a sign, passes through the line, and warns: 'Prepare well for this bird.' They come prepared, gather their ranks, and stand ready over it.

Among the signs that the Sheikh mentions: The hoopoe is like a human in that it has a white, clean, and smooth body — its plumage is like fine silk, its coloring is a pale grayish hue, and its size is about that of a sparrow. Its crest is like a small comb. It goes out in the morning and stays outside until sunset, and for seven nights after sunset it remains — like a small partridge — going around and about. And when it lands on the branch of a tree, it settles there in good condition, and its sound is pleasing to those who hear it.

REGARDING THE BAURI FISH: It is said that this fish appeared in the sea at the time of Moses and Joshua, peace be upon them both. At the time when they went to the shore of the sea, a fish came to them and bent its head low in submission. From that time on, the fish became known and is found in the sea. Its length is more than a span of a hand, and on one side it has bones and thorns, and on the other side it has good qualities. All of its roasted flesh looks just like a perfectly roasted piece of fish. The Jews gather them, dry them, and send them as gifts to other lands.

REGARDING THE BAURI FISH (second account): There is a fish called Ba'l, which is found in all the seas. I saw a fish like it and was extremely frightened and terrified. The sound of its voice alone causes a man's heart to burst. From its foulness the seawater becomes greatly disturbed, causing one to drown in fear. It is said that when a thousand fish come together seeking to trap and encircle a fish swimming behind it — the Sustainer commands that it be saved from oppression and injustice.

At the confluence of the two seas, a great fish comes, small enough that it escapes and is saved.

The 'Buri' (torpedo/ray): This creature has a body shaped like a felt cap; it has a male head, no eyes and no mouth. Inside it there hangs something like a piece of flesh suspended, resembling a swallowing sac. When a smaller fish approaches it as prey, it moves violently and the area around it turns black like squid ink. Those who see it think that the blackness is something fierce and predatory, but when the creature seizes them the surroundings become like a bubble and it does not dissolve or shake. From it one extracts a substance used to make ink — it produces the finest ink, such that it neither spreads nor bleeds; it is both black and bright.

And as for the Swordfish (Shawl Balıq): It is said that it resembles a channel or canal. It has two fins on its back. It rises from the depths, leaps above the water, soars through the air, and then plunges back into the sea.

And as for this: It is a fish called the Manara (lighthouse fish), long and thick. It rises from the water and, eating only itself, sinks. People have approached it, and it is said that drums, trumpets, and pipes were played for it, and tablets of law were brought—efforts were made to tame it—yet some large fish found among them are well known.

And as for this: It is a fish such that when the water recedes on a shoal it remains there for up to six hours. It is compelled and agitated, writhing and turning, seeking to find its way back to the deep sea. It has two fins on each side, large and wide like the wings of a great bird. And as for this Swordfish: it tears apart whatever comes near it. Those around it keep moving continually, and whenever they stop they are thrown into turmoil—it is never still and is of a refined nature. And as for this great fish: its length exceeds twenty cubits, and people believe that it is the whale (fīl fish) in which they think things are stored.

From this one, with knife and dagger, its keeper passes days; in various forms appearances emerge and its beauty and elegance are transferred in the copy of Kemi. A STORY: Greetings — Tercan has spoken at the appointed time:

In the time of the Caliphate, having seen his companion, he sent him to find Alexander. Having sought and found Ibn Sal and the Caliph's greetings, Tercan was sent to see him. He stayed in that direction for several days. The story tells that in that first land, a creature that hunts fish, wrapping its fins, tied with rope, was dragged to the shore. From among them emerged one of beautiful face, with long hair, dark eyes, and a silver-white body, smooth as a polished surface. She cried out and pressed her two hands against her face, clinging to her captors. They released her, marveling at her grace and elegance. She dove back and disappeared beneath the water. The people who had gathered there were astonished, and so the tale came to its end.

And on land: its young are born in the sea, and it raises them until they grow into a great cloud. It brings them up from the depths of the sea, raising them like a great fish in nature, and when it strikes lightning, it is like dry fire on a tree or upon something it alights upon, it destroys it. And its rank is such that when it approaches, the cloud lifts its name, and it is said to be Gog and Magog, and do not flee from them. Their food becomes of such a quantity that it brings and cuts it into pieces in the sea, and they feed upon it — so it has been recorded.

On land animals and sea animals: a detailed account based on the story of this region's people.

The peoples of Iran would come and raid and plunder, and the Ajam (Persians) and the Shamlu (a tribe) were greatly distressed by this matter.

When the period of Nushirwan's reign arrived, he decided that the land of Iran should be secured and protected from the Turks.

At an auspicious hour he laid the foundation, and began the construction. But before the military forces had finished building the wall — gate by gate, completing the entire structure —

he was exceedingly glad, and at the very spot where the first stone was laid, he set up his throne.

So great was he that he contemplated the meaning of this achievement, and prostrated himself in gratitude, saying:

"I have now attained my comfort," and went to rest. Nushirwan retired to that resting place.

But suddenly a wondrous creature of strange appearance manifested itself, coming from the direction of his frontier guards, and Nushirwan's soldiers saw it and resolved to hunt it down.

Nushirwan rose up and asked: "What is this commotion?" They told him a creature had appeared. Nushirwan commanded: "Put down your weapons — do not disturb the creature that has come to our settlement, for it has led us to build this great wall."

The weapons of the sultan's army were laid down. The creature came before Nushirwan's throne and said:

"O just king! In this land there are many creatures like me. I am one of them; I have been guiding you so that you would build here. I was commanded by revelation: go to this man, and tell him to build here and tend to it."

Once it had given news of the event, it disappeared from sight and went away on its own. Whether it had fallen into a pit, or crossed a bridge, or been struck down, or joined [others], [is unknown].

And all water animals are of two kinds: one kind is like fish, which cannot subsist except in water; and the other kind is such that they can live both on dry land — like sheep — sustaining themselves in water, and also outside in the air sustaining themselves [both in water and on land].

[Marginalia in red:] All water animals are of two kinds.

Those who breathe through inhalation [i.e., air-breathing creatures] have no need to hold their breath, and those who live in the countryside [on land] need to breathe through inhalation. If one holds one's breath under water using only the lungs, one will perish. And since aquatic animals have no voice, it is as if they do not exist.

The Almighty God placed heat in the nature of aquatic animals to repel the cold of the waters. They live and move about, but if they were to leave the water they would perish, for the heat of their nature acts upon them, and being deprived of inhaling cold water would cause their death. Divine wisdom has decreed that every animal should have limbs and joints suited to it, and that the bodily members of each animal should be proportionate to its body, and that it should have a skin and vessel suited to its own preservation. Among aquatic creatures, there are very many shells and husks, and for this reason, from pearl oysters and cocoons, He clothed them without garments in abundance. And some He created with fins and tails so that they swim in water, and some He created with feet so that they walk on land. Some He made eaters and some He made food, so that some eat others, and He increased [their number] so that they would be of benefit to humans. So there is no need to be anxious about the sustenance of animals, for the power and wisdom of God Almighty, exalted be His glory, has no limit.

I have described the animals in alphabetical order and explained the properties of each. If some repetition occurs in the discussion, 'Repetition is good [when it brings benefit].'

The Letter Alif

The Sea Hare (Arnab al-Bahr) — that is to say, the creature called 'sea-rabbit': this is an animal about which Ibn Sina (Abu Ali) has said it is an animal whose parts, like the leaves of a plant, are incorporated within it. Its ashes, when applied before the onset of alopecia (dā' al-tha'lab), are especially beneficial when used with its own fat. When applied as a poultice, it removes cataracts and brightens the vision. If it is used as a collyrium or applied as kohl, it kills instantly, for it is deadly — it is equal to an open wound. Abu Ali and other physicians have said that it purges the bile and brightens the sight.

The Hare (al-Tays) — this word in its original meaning signifies a formidable creature. It resembles in form, as has been described, something quite awe-inspiring. The large wild asses found in the steppe and the sea creatures can be hunted. It is most suitable for good hunting, and among its properties: if two persons who are enemies of one another each eat of it, their thunder and their voices will resound in harmony.

If the teeth of snakes are among the colors and remain, they cause harm (damage/incidents).
At that time, when it passes through the water, God Almighty, exalted be He, has sent a bird—
it resembles a partridge. That bird is said to have bones (a kind of marrow) in it.
Those birds enter the afflicted area; the first of their kind and their evils intend to attack the crocodile. When an enemy appears, that bird calls out, the crocodile is warned by it and throws itself into the water and escapes.
The bird cleans the crocodile from leeches; after it has done so, sometimes the crocodile opens its mouth. The bird goes inside the crocodile's mouth, and the crocodile's throat-worm (parasite) and the marrow inside it—the crocodile swallows it upward.
It pulls and stretches, catches the bird in its jaw and swallows it, and the crocodile remains in the Nile without harm.
And in the rivers, it also happens that at the bank of the Nile, when the blood-colored water appears, humans or animals who see it, coming to the bank, are seized and constrained, and at the right moment the crocodile emerges from the water, repels them with force, and they scatter.
It is said among its properties and wonders: if a person's eye is diseased, if it is the right eye, then take its right eye, and if it is the left eye, then take its left eye, place it as a compress on the eye—
it will become well. It helps carry what the afflicted person bears; it benefits one struck by epilepsy.
Whoever keeps a piece of it in their home, it keeps away insects and calms the household. Applying its fat soothes the place. Its bile, if dropped into the eyes, removes the pain that has fallen into the eyes. Its dung also has benefits. And a piece cut from its skin, God the Exalted...

Giving thanks, not a single army could overcome it, and it prevails over everything, and the covenant rests upon the Almighty.

The sanbān [a sea creature]: This animal lives in the depths of the sea; its body is large, its length is great, and it has sharp teeth; its eyes are wide and its mouth is huge; its belly cannot be filled; it devours sea creatures. When it moves, it is as if the sea is in turmoil — no ship can escape from it in reality; entire fleets are struck by it and destroyed. Then Almighty God sends an angel who comes and drives it back into the deep, returning it. Another sea creature: God Almighty commands, sending an angel who draws it up from the sea near the land of Gog and Magog, where it feeds on very little food. Someone has related this story.

In the place of Gurdbar there are two great serpents (dragons), each of considerable size. One resembles a leopard in its coloring, and its body is like that of fish piled upon fish, and it has great fins like the fins of a fish, and its head has the appearance of a human face — do not be deceived by its likeness! It has ears like the ears of a human, and great round eyes each as large as a great circular basin. From its back six more dragons have appeared, each one of twenty columns (coils), and each dragon carried its young upon itself.

This is the image of a dragon that has dragon-like heads.

As for its properties — that is to say, if the fat from the place where the dragon has pressed down upon something is applied (as a remedy), it will be beneficial.

And it is said that near it [the creature] great courage appears, and whoever smears himself with its fat, the group of enemies will be repelled, and a woman takes pleasure beyond measure from it, it is said.

The Jirri [eel-like fish]: It is produced from the union of a snake and a river fish called Baloch-jama. It kills small snakes, and if a small snake comes to the water's edge to drink, the Jirri hides in the water, grabs the snake by its tail and drags it in. It is permissible to eat according to religious law.

[Illustration of a fish]

Whoever is bitten by it, if one applies remedies and recites [incantations] over the afflicted limb, and someone skilled speaks pleasing words, the person recovers and does not die from eating it again. It gives strength to the body, and the vapors it produces are beneficial for nasal ailments. It relieves pain. It is also known to be beneficial, as has been said.

Halka [another fish]: with short vowel on the lam — it lives under the ground like a snake. It comes out at the end of the day seeking food, creeping near small streams, enters the water, swallows blood, and becomes agitated.

Eating eel with it — its property is this: that the woman who eats it will become fertile.
[Illustration: a long pink fish (eel) swimming in blue water]
Dolphin (Delfin): This is a blessed fish of the sea. If it befriends a person at sea and that person is drowning, it takes him on its back and brings him to shore; and if someone is about to drown, it comes and by pressing its tail allows them to grasp it and saves them. Its benefit in relation to the stars is described [elsewhere].
Shrimp (Rubyan): It is a small fish. Among its properties is this: if the tip of a thorn has broken off in a limb, place shrimp over it; cook chickpeas with it and give them to the person who has the thorn inside — let him eat them and it will draw out the foreign body. It greatly increases sexual vigor and nourishment. Cook its broth and mix it with whey (qara su); the mucilage produced from it is beneficial for half-headache (migraine) and for cracked lips.
Torpedo Ray (Ra'ada): [Pronounced with] opening of the ra' and doubling of the 'ayn — it is a type of fish found mostly in the sea of Egypt. Its body is small but it is extremely numbing. Its property is this: when a fisherman's net fills [with fish], they know the freshness of the water by whether the torpedo ray is alive or not. They tie it with a rope to a tamarisk tree until that fish dies, and after that its numbing property disappears, and the physicians say its broth greatly [increases something — text continues]...

Hot substances are applied to [certain] harmful places. Regarding tuna fish: if a woman takes some of it and gives it to a man without his knowing, and if a man gives it to a woman without her knowing, those women too will feel love [for them]. The tobalıq fish, found in the depths of the sea, whose head causes pain — placing it near the ear is said to relieve headache. Some scholars deduce from its preparation a treatment for headache pain, and it is said to relieve [it]. Galen accepted this view. Zamor is a type of fish, the most numerous kind, found alive in the world. It is a blessed creature; it is said to be present at blessed [events]. When it opens its mouth it is like the position of one who places burdens [on others]. If [this fish] intends harm toward another fish, it enters through its ear into its brain and eats it, until at last that fish, throwing it off from its hand, strikes it against the rocks and destroys it. Afterward, from that fish's ear — Safinas is a type of fish found in the region of Jerusalem. Sheikh Abu Ali [Ibn Sina] said: the ash of its body, placed on the eyes of animals, removes [film from] their sight. Saratan [crab]: it has pincers at its head, eight legs on its sides, and moves sideways. The torpedo fish: among the sea creatures, one that passes through water — it has two passages, one cold and one warm. When it passes through the warm passage it becomes weak; when it comes to the cold passage, it becomes feeble and exhausted, showing its weakness and helplessness, so that it does no harm. Then [when passing through] the open passage, it returns by that route [recovering its strength].

When it enters and derives nourishment from within, it is as though a strong vessel carries its fluid to the channels that seek sustenance for the living, causing it to flow toward the tree-roots below, striking and driving into iron and thorns that have lodged there, and it is beneficial in that place for the man who is bitten by it and whose foot is swollen. If it is placed in cold water and the body is bathed with it, it becomes beneficial; and if one who has found it keeps it with him, it will protect him from celestial afflictions. If one washes something with it and wraps it, it will cause abrasions to heal; and if it is put into a vessel and the white that forms on it is applied to the eyes of those who suffer from eye ailments, it will cure them and restore sight to those who have lost it. If it is ground up with pig fat and applied, then dissolved in water and drunk, it will be beneficial for paralysis. Its thorns, if iron or a thorn has pierced the flesh and become lodged, are effective for drawing it out — it has been said that it benefits those afflicted with tuberculosis, and if tied over the eyes it cures them; if tied over those afflicted with scrofula, for as long as it remains there the pain will be relieved; and its planetary properties have been noted.

SKINK (saqanqūr): The crocodile skink — when it is rubbed, if it is given in water to someone who has no children, that person will be cured and become fertile; and if it is put in water and a man passes by it, he will have offspring.

If one rubs the first organ (the genitals) with it (the skink/saqanqur) and applies it, a man will find health. And if the skink is placed in water and a man rubs himself with that water afterward, he will find health from the skink. Its general nature is stimulating, and especially its head part is extremely nourishing in its essence, and its specific property is very strengthening — it increases the vitality to a degree that horses too benefit. However, one must bind it firmly and hold it carefully, and look after one's health by rubbing it on the face; it removes blemishes and spots, drives away tooth pain, strengthens the eyesight of animals, and with kohl (antimony) applied to the eyes it removes opacity and film from the eye.

Turtle (Sulhafat): It is an amphibious creature, living both in the sea and on land. But the sea variety grows very large, and it sometimes brings its back out of the sea onto the shore, so that travelers who see it mistake it for an island and dismount onto it (thinking it is land).

Story: A shepherd tells the story of how he once went to the sea and came upon a turtle...

It is clear and bright, and it is said that this fish has a great collective power; it benefits people. It purifies the river water. With honey and without food, if one eats it at night — the Sunbut (or 'Sanbut'), which is this fish, is seen in the sea coast areas. It is delicate, slender in body and broad in girth, and lives a long time. The young of this fish cannot be separated; they stay close and hold together, and turn away. Its male calls out in a voice like that of a young ram, and its call can be heard for thirty lengths of a field. It leaps through the air, and is counted among the fish. Under 'Shaftan' — it is a creature of wondrous form, different from all other fish. Its body is multicolored, and its two heads resemble those of a mare; it has front limbs. Between its ribs there is something lean and slender, and immediately it settles [the ailment].

[Section heading: Picture of the Shaftan]

Sayr (Sayr-fish): It is a small fish; the people of Syria call it by the name 'Listamiya.' Its water, when used for gargling, removes ulcers and inflammation from the throat.

Dafda' (Frog): It is a creature that lives both in water and on land. It is generated in stagnant and corrupted waters.

[Marginal headings: Letter Sad / Letter Shin]

From those (creatures) straight as an arrow, the thin yellowish-white ones and the black-haired ones come from them. After that, the middle ones of the group come, then after coming from them, one who surpasses the others in detail and investigation is this: Among the community those who wander and roam, and who have gathered and assembled in the places of the land, live among the groups that dwell there. The group that cannot stay (in one place), the air there keeps them moving. Through it God Almighty repels (harm), and from that, the creatures that have not yet been created — those who pass among them year after year — greatly increase in number. In that year, plagues occur, and the (creature's) night-vigil and its alarm have this quality: it is pulled out from the water, and if it does not come out, and the green (variety) of it appears, it indicates corruption for the person who consults about it. It drives away and keeps at bay, removing the harmful effects, and the (creature) placed in the water where it is found benefits those who drink it. If a lion releases the creature, and someone buys or sells bound to it, they will benefit, and the female of the creature — they say — if the eyes of the one who looks at it are dark, and the blue-eyed one appears, and the safety of the graves increases, their branches shed, and (it has) benefit for the chest. And cooking it thoroughly — a woman who has a bad condition, when she looks at her state, it will be removed from her. Bilyas the Physician said: If the creature's interior is placed firmly in this manner, be wary of the one suspected. If it is given to someone and is placed near a nursing woman, and applied to her chest at midday, it will hold.

They say that if one wants to purify salt flats of reeds, one should spread the ash of reed-stems along the banks, then gather the waterside reeds and pull them out clean. Then, after tying them in bundles and floating them on the water, the frogs will be drawn together thinking it is dry land and will climb upon them; in this way the frogs are cleverly caught and removed from the pond.

The Peacock. Abu Hamid relates: I heard from a trustworthy elder of the sea-coast that he once saw near the sea a peacock more beautiful than any peacock he had ever encountered in form and coloring — it spread its wings, bent its neck, and began to preen itself. Then, following along, he drew nearer to see it, but before he could reach it the bird suddenly opened its beak and let out a cry; and its cry was unlike any other he had ever heard.

Leech [ʿAlaq] — with the voweling of 'ayn and lam — is a creature that lives in water, generated in rivers. When physicians wish to draw blood from a limb, they bring this leech to that limb so that it attaches and draws out that blood. When they have finished with it, they place it on coarse salt immediately upon completion, so it releases and falls off. Then they dry those [leeches] and place them over a sore, filling it completely with them.

First: Among the stones found [in this region] is the Syrian stone — note how remarkable it is. Its like has been known to kill people: if one of them dies inside a glass vessel, what comes after it becomes harmful; then it is collected and rubbed, and one smears [the affected part] with it, so that the hair falls out entirely from that spot.

Bone [ʿAẓm, highlighted in red]: It is a category among the hundred-footed creatures found in local waters and in rivers — of the genus narcissus-spikenard. It is also found in the land. It is a most wondrous creature: it has a shell on its back, one hundred legs, and extremely delicate ears, eyes, and veins. When a person places a shell-trap for it and it emerges and wanders about, it recognizes its own shell, for spikenard blooms, and fumigating with it benefits epilepsy; rubbing its ash on the teeth polishes them. Rubbing the ash of its feathers and fur on a wound is especially beneficial.

Water-Horse [Faras al-Mā'] — it is a mare that lives in the water. However, its mane and its snorting come from it...

Very long and fine of body, with a smooth gait, small-headed, without a branching mark, larger than a donkey and smaller than a horse — it is found in the sea, and when it comes out it mates with a mare of the region, and from it a foal of extraordinary beauty is produced.

— STORY —

Shaykh Abu al-Qasim of Karkegan says: Once, on the shore of the sea, he had tied his own mare overnight. Suddenly, out of the sea, a black stallion emerged and mounted his mare and coupled with her, and from that union a foal was produced, which was exceedingly beautiful. When Shaykh Abu al-Qasim came there later, he found the foal. That horse had come out of the sea, mounted the mare, and produced a foal; then it returned to the sea. And the foal, being killed shortly after, was thrown into the sea, and the foal too was cast into the sea — and that was the end of the matter.

— The Shaykh at that moment went to that place, as if the horse-keeper had come —

Shaykh Abu al-Qasim said to the companions and the devotees: "Wherever you find a wild ass running free, note it." It is said that its hoof-marks are beneficial: that is, if someone has pain in the belly, if he carries its opposite tooth, the pain will immediately be relieved. And if its bones are burned and the smoke is applied to the groin area as a fumigation, it will expel excess humors; and if applied to a cancerous wound, it will prevent the disease of cancer; and it will dry up the flowing sores and harden them; and if its bile is administered to someone suffering from jaundice, health will be obtained. And if it is buried in the corner of a village or at its boundary, the plagues and pestilences that descend upon that place will be averted.

And when it is burned and the ash is placed upon a swelling, it calms it and repels it.

Qatus [Qatus fish]: It is like a large fish, and when its pieces come near, it is certain that it will swallow those who approach it. Women whose menstruation has ceased [use it as medicine]... and drops flow from it.
A great fish, at one level, pulls away what comes near it and drives away evil spirits from upon [those afflicted].
Its fat, when applied as a coating to the body of Bursa [or: a person with skin condition], removes diseases and ailments. The Qunduz [beaver] is an animal of both land and water, found also in great rivers. It has two sacs [castoreum glands], one towards the water side and one towards the dry side. When it senses danger from one direction, it runs in the other direction. Its burrow is elevated, and it uses its teeth to cut trees. The right side of its offspring [is used for medicine], and those who serve it [or: its servants] feed on fish. Those who are attendants [subordinates] — their skins are taken by their masters from the walnut/pine trees and stripped of their hairs. At night, those who are served [masters] eat fish, and their constitution becomes complete and excellent, and [it brings] benefit to their body, as the book of India records.

The north wind (Saba) is beneficial [in certain conditions]. Drinking it mixed with rose-water syrup is also beneficial for palsy, hemiplegia, thick phlegm, killing black bile, tremors, fever, reptiles, the animal called Suf'a, and similar creatures — this is considered authoritative.

The Water Marten (Fandhalmā') resembles a cat in appearance; the front part of its head is black, and it is of the fish-eating kind. It is a great species, varying in size from small to large; its color is black, its flesh is pleasant in taste and nutritious. Its liver is beneficial [medicinally]. If its white skin is used to make a drum, and that drum is beaten, the wild vermin and insects of the earth that hear its sound will die.

QŪNĪ (Ram-fish / Unicorn Fish)
This is a type of fish found in the sea of Baklashdeh [a certain sea region]. It has a single horn on its head, and because of this it is called Qūnī. A great creature lives there, and whenever this fish swims near it, that creature rears up and splits the fish apart, piece by piece, consuming its flesh. It feeds on it, and likewise many other sea creatures gather around the remains. It is said that in that sea, when a great person intends to cross, this horn rises up and destroys [him]. And sometimes this horn strikes and splits apart those who pass by, drowning them, and it feeds on them. Every boat that crosses that sea, its sailors take precautions, for this horn breaks the ship.

KALB AL-MĀ' (The Water-Dog / Sea-Dog)
This is a well-known creature whose arms are short and whose legs are long, with a head resembling a dog's. Its body is like a fish, so that it resembles a crocodile mixed with a fish. It is said to be quite capable: it enters the water, ambushes fish, catches them, and kills them. Its horn — some say it strikes and wounds; others say that its skin is needed — it is said among them that its skin is useful. It is noted that its skin is needed for its [medicinal or practical] purpose, and it is unlike the skin of other creatures.
