The hunters cannot benefit [from it]; whoever finds its nest and strikes the eggs, and the hunter comes back, the bow burns it and it perishes. Striking its egg and eating its dung causes it to show [a remedy]; as for its brain, it repels the darkness of the eye and its measure is like that of the panther; it is firm in the marrow. From the oil of its elbows and knees, it causes dryness; from its direction, the teeth of the animals are beneficial and proven for the treatment of children; it is well-known that it cures those in the places where the disease of mange occurs, and the disease of mange disappears.

[Marginal note in red:] Image of the dog

The weasel (gūsaj) is a type found in the Persian sea, described and illustrated in detail. It is found in most seas and in their vicinity, living in gardens; it hunts at night when it finds a garden and hunts abundantly, and during the day it does not hunt. The fifth observation: it is upon the earth, and there are a few seasons in it. The first is that it is truly upon the earth, rather its body is simple, cold and dry in nature.

The moving body in its middle, while the center of the heavens is at rest — in its revolution one should not say that it inclines to one side, for this reason it is similar: if one were to suppose that it moves, for example, from East to West, like the movement of one who walks, one would see only so much as one sees — for it is not as though it disappears and returns — one would see it as it stands at an orderly distance, such that one sees the mirror of seventy-three farsakhs as one degree, and it appears as a mirror.

Some say there are two witnesses, meaning four directions: one East, one West, one South, one North. Some say it stands upright like a balance, others say it is like a drum, and some say it is like a flat circle — all of these amount to saying that the Earth is spherical, and its center is at the center of the celestial spheres, and ultimately, as the scholar said: a solar eclipse taken as a single reference but appearing differently, except where it may be accepted — in the eastern and western lands, for example, in one place at the beginning of the night one sees it, and in another place at half the night one sees it. If the difference of rising and setting were at one time, then all places in relation to the eclipse would be the same — if the earth were spherical, it would not differ. If the eclipse occurs in all lands, then if the earth is spherical, it would not differ.

Second Chapter: On the properties of the Earth — but first, let it be known that in the First Chapter some rulings were mentioned. It is appropriate to mention here, in connection with it, the remaining rulings — that the Earth is situated at the center of the celestial sphere. Pythagoras the philosopher held that the Earth, the seas, the celestial sphere and the stars are stationary, and that it is their revolution around them, and from this revolution the refutation of the like thereof is apparent — for if one were to set the Earth in motion toward any direction and release it, it would be necessary that its destination not be reached.

For this Earth, as the most eminent of the wise have correctly stated — namely Ptolemy — the Earth is stationary at the center of the celestial sphere, and the sphere attracts it on all sides just as a magnet attracts iron. And since it is perfectly centered, the subtle celestial sphere does not attract the dense Earth but rather repels it, because the Earth's distance from the sphere is equal in all directions with respect to the celestial bodies. The distance of the sphere from the Earth is not unequal in any direction, as those knowledgeable in geometry will understand — to some this seems like a paradox, but it is as we have described. The nature of the Earth's being at the center is required by all cosmic bodies, and divine wisdom has so ordained it, that the Earth, being cold and dry, is suited to receive those qualities, so that it might generate minerals and plants. It is capable of producing gold and other precious things — for if gold were not produced, the benefits derived from it would not be obtained. It is surrounded on all sides to a certain extent by water, just as the surface of water encloses what is beneath it. But not entirely — only that amount which emerges from the water and forms mountains, deserts, caves, plains, valleys, rivers, cities, and villages — a certain proportion of the land where plants and animals exist. The Earth is uniform in its parts, and the sun causes heat and movement to appear upon it in a known manner, and unique properties appear therein. In a concise account, it has properties found nowhere else — for example, certain precious stones are formed within it such as rubies and emeralds, and the virtue of the soil produces all manner of plants.

And from these causes [the soil] is formed, and from the dust that settles, the earth is made. Humans, too, are created from soil — and since they leave different traces in reality, you can observe that some are learned scholars, some are devout worshippers, some are skilled in one craft and others in another craft entirely. The benefit fitting for each person is there: for the scholars and the worshippers, the benefit lies in the blessing of prayer and devotion, and for the craftsmen, in their craft. Know that the true nature of the earth and all that is within it — the knowledge that encompasses this is beyond measure, for the detailed knowledge belongs to God alone, since God Most High encompasses all things: 'Not a leaf falls but that He knows it, and no grain in the darknesses of the earth, and nothing moist or dry, but that it is written in a clear record.' The secrets and wisdom of God are without limit; as has been mentioned, this discussion is a summary. If one is granted divine guidance, the door of wisdom opens to the heart, and one arrives at understanding. Third Chapter: On the size of the body of the Earth. Know that Abu al-Rayhan [al-Biruni] stated that the length of the Earth is one thousand one hundred and sixty-three farsakhs and one-third of a farsakh, and its circumference is six thousand seven hundred farsakhs. The area of the surface of the Earth, outside [the oceans], is fourteen thousand seven hundred and four thousand in addition — four thousand separate, two hundred and some farsakhs — and four thousand more, two hundred farsakhs, two farsakhs and a fifth of a farsakh. The surveyors say: if one digs into the earth like a well, to the depth of one hundred [units], for example — [and thus through the layers of the earth] — and the Commander of the Faithful, the Caliph al-Ma'mun, in his time ordered the earth to be measured by calculating the elevation of the pole star, degree by degree across the sky, and it turned out to be sixty-six and two-thirds miles per degree. And Ptolemy said that the size of the Earth can be determined by the [observation of the] sun.

Regarding the risings and settings considered according to the four divisions of the day and the canonical hours (sa'at): 

To expand upon this, scholars say there are four numbers (divisions), as the ancients held — so for example, thirty degrees equals two farsakhs. 

Fourth Chapter: On the layers of the earth — that is to say, the land. 

The scholars say: Upon the earth there is a line of virtue and excellence, through lands I have mentioned, which are equal one to another — the southern and northern are called [meridians]. That first line is called the Equatorial Circle (dā'irat al-mu'addil al-nahār) and the Line of the Equator (khatt al-istiwā'). 

This line, considered as drawn through the middle of the equator, extends toward the east and the west. Because of this, that line is called east and west. The world is divided at this point into four quarters: two quarters are northern and two quarters are southern — the northern quarter being one. 

Beyond the water is what is called the Inhabited Quarter (rub' al-maskūn), and those three quarters are covered by the sea that surrounds [the earth]. Not all of the Inhabited Quarter is populated; rather, some parts are inhabited. This is because in this quarter there are seas, mountains, deserts, wildernesses, and ruins. 

In the direction closest to the south, in the extreme regions, neither plants nor animals exist. And in the direction of the extreme north, likewise, little vegetation or animal life exists — indeed almost nothing at all. The scholars, according to their reckoning regarding the sphere of the earth and its middle regions, say this is understood and established. 

As for what is reported from 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them both: he said that the Almighty God placed the earth upon [His] eye; and the eye upon a fish; and the fish is in the water; and the water upon a rock; and the rock upon the back of an angel.

"And the first angel holds it [the earth] suspended — that is, it is suspended in its substances, standing by the power of God Most High."

[Right margin note:] "Why with one sovereign angel" / "Depiction of the body [held] by the sovereign angel"

Fifth Chapter: On the Seven Climates (Aqālīm) of the Inhabited Quarter (Rab' al-Maskūn), from East to West — the Bulgars

They divided [the inhabited quarter] into seven parts and called each part a 'climate' (iqlīm), laying it out as a basis for understanding. From east to west across the Seven Climates, the length runs from east to west, and the breadth from south to north. However, the length and breadth of each climate differ considerably. In the first climate, the length from east to west is three thousand farsakhs, and the breadth from south to north is approximately sixty farsakhs — it is therefore the shortest. In the seventh climate, the length from east to west is one thousand five hundred farsakhs, and the breadth is sixty farsakhs. The remaining climates in between differ in their lengths and breadths. The division of the inhabited quarter into seven climates is not a truly precise division; rather, it is a conventional arrangement established by rulers and kings to define territorial boundaries so that those who know them may identify them. The first [founders of this system] were — the kings: [Alexander,] Ardashir, and Babak. And [concerning] the Bulgars — first we shall mention certain introductory matters, after which we shall describe the climates one by one in detail, so that from this [work] one may find the climates, their cities, rivers, seas, and wonders all assembled.

First Introduction: Know that 'world' means the place of settlement, for without permanence and population it cannot be inhabited.

The matter is this: the peoples known as Gog and Magog ruled [a region]; they are the descendants of Japheth son of Noah. As Dīnār Āshtakhātī wrote in his book, describing in detail how they spread across [the land] — and [also] the descendants of Ham son of Noah [spread] in various tribes and peoples of many kinds — and their [further] branches [are as follows]...

...the West, reaching its end, and those [lands] are distant from the other kingdoms.
Some of the Hindus say that the inhabited earth [extends] from the equatorial line by one hundred and sixty-four
degrees of the celestial sphere, and the rest is ruined in terms of cultivation, agriculture, and animals,
because the extreme heat of the sea prevents settlement — for that is the first climate —
and the second and some of the third [climates], and in the seventh climate it is extremely cold,
while the remainder is temperate. The Second Introduction: God Most High created [man] in such a way
that, unlike other animals, he is not capable of sustaining himself alone; rather, by necessity,
he is brought together here: food, if clothing is to be obtained together with it.
Do you not see that most food depends on agriculture, and agriculture depends on tools,
and the tools of trade depend on the ironsmith, and most clothing depends on the plowman,
and on the cotton-carder, and on the spinner, and on the fuller, and on the tailor?
No single person is capable of mastering all these crafts, and in suitable places
one after another, villages and cities are built and people gather together.
Kings therefore wish to build cities for their subjects,
and [the narrative] returns to say: they chose the most noble of places, and upon them built edifices,
producing [settlements] in the most noble of locations, where those of sound disposition dwell, and those whose minds
are upright. But as for those of corrupt temperament, they find no rest in those places, and an evil exit
arrives for them.

The disruption of reason and the variation of moral character and order is discussed in the Third Introduction, as they say: In the earth there are four directions: East, West, South, and North. The extremities of these directions are blameworthy, either due to the intensity of heat or the excess of cold, so that what is wholesome is only a small portion of the earth—for example, the Third Climate and the middle of the Fourth Climate and the Fifth Climate. As for the others, their inhabitants are as though tormented, as if they were in a kind of hellfire or icy coldness. This is the Fourth Introduction, as they have said:

Spacious dwellings suit the world and their inhabitants find comfort in them, yet they weaken the innate vital heat and cause the spirit to dissolve. Those who dwell in such places have weakened bodies, timid hearts, feeble strength, and diminished industry. This is because cold dwellings harden the bodies of their inhabitants, block the pores, strengthen the innate heat, nourish those who dwell in them, harden their bodies, and instill in them courage and strength, which is why their resolve is firm.

However, the air of moderate dwellings is neither too harsh nor too mild; those who dwell in them are near to balance, their temperaments are supple and receptive to influence, quick, yet their strength is given to some lethargy. But dry dwellings block the passages and dry out the bodies, so that those who dwell there have dry brains and heated strength. As for dwellings of rocky terrain, the air there is sharp, biting, and cold, so that...

The natures of those people become hardened, and in them arise bad character, arrogance, and independence in their affairs, while courage becomes part of their temperament. The Fifth Introduction: Concerning all minerals, all plants, and the various kinds of animals — not every one of them exists everywhere.

As for minerals: Gold, for example, is found only in lands where there are sandy deserts and mountains. Silver, copper, lead, and iron are found only where the soil is mixed with rocks. Sulfur is found only in fiery (volcanic) lands. Salt-peter (nitre) is found only in moist lands. Salt is found only around salt-marshes. Alum and gall-oak extract are found only in fine soils. Tar and naphtha are found only in places with oily soils.

As for plants: Banana and plantain grow only in hot countries — there also grow pomelo, orange, pomegranate, and lemon. Their growth requires intense heat. Walnut, almond, and pistachio grow only in cold countries. Reeds grow only along riverbanks and in well-watered places. Acacia (henna-tree) and mimosa grow only in dry, barren lands. The lote-tree grows in the plains. Cloves grow only on certain islands. Indian coconut, ginger, and turmeric grow only in the lands of India. Teak and ebony grow only in Yemen and its surrounding lands.

As for animals: The elephant, for example, lives in India, and those born and raised there live longer than those born elsewhere, and their dispositions...

...and they are long-necked; the giraffe is found in the lands of Abyssinia, and the buffalo is found in hot countries. Sable, marten, and musk deer are found in the eastern and northern lands, and the saker falcon and the hobby are found only in the highlands. The ostrich and the sandgrouse and the bustard lay their eggs only in the open plains and deserts. Ducks and the rest of the waterfowl lay their eggs along the banks of rivers, beside lakes, and at the water's edge, as do the heron and the kingfisher. The nightingale lays its eggs only in gardens, and the magpie only in the highlands. This account of the birds is contrary to what was said at the outset and noted by the learned. Now I will describe the seven climes one by one in order, and I will mention the places therein letter by letter in alphabetical order, God Almighty willing.

The First Clime — This clime is under the dominion of Saturn. At the beginning of this clime, from the equatorial line, the meridian altitude of Capricorn and the pole are equal; toward its end the meridian altitude is two degrees and three-quarters. Its eastern extremity is in the land of China; from there one passes through the island of Serendib (Sri Lanka) and, crossing the sea southward, reaches the Arabian Peninsula; then crossing the Red Sea one reaches the land of Abyssinia and the Nile of Egypt; then crossing the western lands one reaches its middle, where the land of Sanaa is situated.

Hadhramaut: along its shores to the south lie the lands of Aden, and along one of its shores to the north lies Tihama, which is near Mecca. At the beginning of this region the length of the day is twelve and a half hours, in the middle it is thirteen hours, and at its end it is thirteen hours and a quarter. Since some of the conditions of this clime have now been mentioned, from here onward I will describe the cities of this clime in alphabetical order.

Iram Dhat al-Imad: This city lies between Sanaa and Hadhramaut. It is related that Shaddad ibn 'Ad, one of the mighty tyrants, built it. When he heard that God the Most High was preparing Paradise for His righteous servants, he resolved to look upon it, saying: 'I too will found a city like unto Paradise.' For this purpose he appointed a thousand overseers under whose authority there were a thousand men. He commanded them to choose from the earth the finest site available, and then to build thereon a great and magnificent city. He ordered that gold and silver be brought and used in its construction, and that some parts be raised above others. Its foundations were of chrysolite and red carnelian, and its upper parts were of pure white stone from underground. He laid out that city with ordered streets and squares, through which rivers flowed. Along the banks of those rivers he paved with gold, and the stones were set with all manner of jewels. Along the banks of the river he caused trees of gold to be planted.

And those like him were accepted from the nobles of that city, and the length of that city was close to ten thousand parasangs, and its width was similar. This Juwaybil lived six hundred years, and in his city he built a lofty palace overlooking the mountain of Maqsur, raised above the plains of Zarnah. Its height was six hundred cubits, and that city, whose soil, when pressed, emitted the scent of saffron, was such that the Prophet was sent to them but they refused to accept his message and persisted in their rebellion. The Prophet threatened them with the punishment of God, and when the building was completed, he himself led seven hundred thousand soldiers, and at one stage's distance, a herald of Samatr raised a great cry, and both he and all the mighty ones and the mountain dwellers perished, until the city was completely hidden, and no one had come to it, and no account of it remained for a time, until a man from Kurd came — his name was Abdullah ibn Qila — who visited it, and the summary of his story is this: He had lost a camel in the region of San'a and while searching for it, he happened to arrive at that city. He went to the land of Syria and presented himself before Mu'awiyah, and showed him with elaborate speech what he had seen in that city. Mu'awiyah summoned Ka'b al-Ahbar and asked him specifically about this matter. He said: 'The one that the Almighty mentions in the Quran — Iram, the city of pillars — was built by Shaddad ibn 'Ad. They say that no one has ever reached it or returned from it.' He said: 'Well then, go and look at this man, and if the description of what you see matches the description of Abdullah ibn Qila, then it is so.'

Mu'awiya affirmed it: the Land of Tibr (Gold) lies in the region of the Land of the Sudan in the West. In the southern part of this province, the heat in these lands is intense, and the people there are lean and thin. Gold is found there in abundance, and among the communities there it is plentiful. In our own lands, the waves rise and fall with the water, and the land faces toward the direction of the rising sun. The gold flows from its sources there, and the people of that land eat taro and small grains. There are many wild animals there, including a great number of leopards, more than in any other land. Camels are scarce there, and finding water is extremely difficult. The people there lack water and when they travel to nearby places, the air shifts and turns. A camel can barely carry a load without tiring. Some camels are not loaded heavily at all, but are sent away thirsty, then when water is found, they are given an abundance of it to drink, and they draw it up and travel swiftly; their riders can no longer keep up with them. The large ones among them kneel down, and the moisture within them — praised be God — moves along, and when they approach water, they fill up quickly and are watered, then driven swiftly onward.

The Land of Abyssinia: This land lies to the north of it. The Gulf of Berbera lies to the south in the direction of the dark land. To its east lie several climates; to the west is the region of Tangier; the heat of that land is intense. The skin of its people is black, owing to the nature of its component parts, and most of them are harmful.

The first Muslims in that region were very few, and the land is long and wide, but the arable area is small. Because rain falls rarely, there is virtually no agricultural produce in the land. Most of the sustenance comes from dates, tamarind, grapes, and pomegranates — these are what the people know. In that land there are wondrous animals such as elephants, giraffes, and rhinoceroses — the rhinoceros being like an ox, except that it is single-horned. Foreigners coming from other lands bind horses as we do. There are many wild elephants there, which people hunt — they are astonishing to behold. They are produced from the union of a wild ox and a serpent — their head is like a camel's head, their horns are small and curved like horns, their teeth are like the small teeth of an elephant, their coloring is like that of a leopard, their legs are like those of a male camel, their small hooves are like the small hooves of a gazelle, their tail is like the tail of an ox, and the giraffe's neck is very long and its haunches are low, and the origin of the giraffe's creation — as certain scholars and authorities have described among the animals mentioned — should be sought in the chapter where it is treated. Since the composition of this book reached the chapter on the Land of Zanj, and its benefits have become accessible to people of learning and discernment, it should be noted that the one who prompted the composition of this aforementioned book and who sowed the seeds of knowledge in the fields of hearts is His Excellency the possessor of felicity in this world and the next, Sultan Mustafa, whose majestic royal countenance came to pass — and he departed from this world to the next.

"And from the Abode of Peace [Baghdad/paradise], the one known as Sururi the Faqir [the poor/humble one], having turned away from others and finished the composition before the book was complete, for the wretched ones who are in need of one good prayer, so that they may receive a good prayer, the matter was indicated. For these [people] a prayer: may God the Exalted bestow mercy, Amen.

The completion of composition occurred in the month of Dhu al-Qa'da, in the year sixty and nine [i.e., 969 AH / approximately 1561–62 CE].
